description: The dispute moved onto X. Means asked Wiles and political adviser James Blair to stop harassing him by text and phone; Blair denied it, calling the complaint a "poor me act" from "a grown man who launched a smear campaign." Within ninety minutes some former MAHA supporters and others in the health freedom movement were arguing the split was staged: Wiles leaving anyway, Means sent out as the good cop, a common enemy to explain two years of little progress. None of this should be treated as fact. Hours later Means published a preservation demand, writing that the two may sue over the Rogan interview and asking them, Ballard Partners, Continental Strategy and others to retain relevant records. No reporting confirms any threat to sue, and the demand is his alone.
title: On X, Means Alleges Harassment and Demands Records Be Preserved, as Some in the Health Freedom Movement Call the Rift Staged

description: Two weeks after resigning as Kennedy's senior adviser, Calley Means sat down with Joe Rogan for episode #2578 and argued that the people Trump pledged to run out of Washington now staff his own White House. He named chief of staff Susie Wiles as the chokepoint, describing a "stranglehold" on policy decisions and saying she had blocked an HHS food initiative out of concern it would cost the party sugar-industry donations. Handed the executive order boosting glyphosate production to review, he says he told them it was a "political disaster," and that Kennedy was cut out of several glyphosate decisions altogether. The New York Times added two further examples from his account: that Wiles's team pushed for more flavored e-cigarette authorizations, a priority for the tobacco companies that gave Republicans at least $20 million during the 2026 cycle, and that the White House bent to a kratom lobbying campaign and softened proposed limits on the products sometimes sold as "gas station heroin." He also faulted political adviser James Blair and pollster Tony Fabrizio for running a midterm operation "obsessed with redistricting." Then he addressed the president directly — "Mr. President, you have suffered. You've been shot to drive significant change" — and offered a prescription: "I would recommend that he clear his house, and I think he's getting there," by "combating special interests, combating the swamp." Hours after the episode posted, Trump announced Wiles was out, replaced by Stephen Miller; no reporting has tied the two events together, and Kennedy thanked her for her "calm and inspiring leadership and wisdom." The White House held its line, spokeswoman Allison Schuster saying "the MAHA coalition has found a champion in President Trump." Blair was blunter about the movement's electoral weight: MAHA "wasn't a top issue to the vast majority of voters. That's not my opinion, that's what voters say in the research." Quotes from the episode are drawn from an unofficial transcript.
title: Calley Means Tells Joe Rogan That Trump Should 'Clear His House' — and Susie Wiles Is Out Hours Later

description: Three Democrats took major races on explicitly health-centred campaigns, in a cycle that otherwise punished MAHA-aligned Republicans. Rob Sand, Iowa's state auditor, beat Zach Lahn for the governorship, the first Democrat to win it in roughly two decades, in a race dominated by the state's climbing cancer rate and farm pollution; he had run since the spring on a cancer task force inside the state health department, restored water quality monitoring, nitrate alerts for drinking water, wider radon testing and a refusal to shield pesticide manufacturers from lawsuits — "We shouldn't be doing immunity for chemical companies that are sickening Iowans." Abdul El-Sayed, a physician and former Detroit health commissioner, took Michigan's Senate seat from Mike Rogers, 52.5 percent to 45.5, and becomes the first Muslim elected to the chamber; he campaigned on Medicare for All as the way to save rural hospitals left exposed by the Republican-led One Big Beautiful Bill Act, working a call and response with crowds — "Money in your …" "Pocket!" "Money out of …" "Politics!" "Medicare for …" "All!" And Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, flipped South Carolina's seat against Darline Graham, appointed after her brother Lindsey Graham's death in July, in a state that had elected no Democratic senator since 1998 and that Trump carried by eighteen points. She ran directly at Kennedy, pledging to "lead the charge to impeach and remove" him and campaigning on the state's measles outbreak and falling herd immunity. "The day that RFK Jr. was nominated to lead HHS," she told The New Republic, "was the day that I really seriously started considering running for this seat."
title: Democrats Win on Health: Sand Flips Iowa, El-Sayed Takes Michigan, Andrews Breaks South Carolina

description: The movement's first real electoral test came with the health agencies visibly struggling. The CDC had shed as much as a third of its workforce while measles spread at record levels; the NIH was left without stable leadership and saw projects stalled, cancelled or censored; the FDA was overstretched by a large cyclosporiasis outbreak. On election day itself New York reported a child's death from measles, the state's first in three decades. Kennedy had cut and disrupted federal vaccine work to hold the most committed part of his base, even as roughly four in ten MAHA voters named healthcare costs as a worry, and in doing so handed his opponents an organising principle: the science advocacy group 3.14 Action called him "our No 1 recruitment and fundraising tool – hands down." Democrats pressed the advantage, running upwards of 158,000 health-related ads against 61,000 from Republicans, with healthcare second among advertising subjects by the Cook Political Report's count. The results followed. MAHA groups made twenty-one endorsements in federal races; eleven of those candidates lost and six won, with four undeclared, and every one of the six wins came in a seat that was never in play. Among the defeated were Zach Lahn in Iowa, where Kennedy had called the governor's race "the most important election going on in this country," and Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall, who chairs the congressional MAHA Caucus. Democrats took the Senate and dozens of House seats, and the candidates who won on something close to the agenda were Democrats, recorded separately on this timeline. Whether MAHA voters follow them there is another question: the movement's grassroots remain loyal to Kennedy and resent how Democrats have treated him, and Zen Honeycutt called the push to impeach him a "colossal mistake."
title: MAHA at a Critical Junction After the Midterms: Agencies in Disarray, Most Endorsed Candidates Lost

description: A U.S. Right to Know report describes CropLife America's 2025 impact review, in which the pesticide trade group ranks its lobbying over the MAHA Commission above everything else it did that year. The commission's May 2025 findings had singled out glyphosate and atrazine and questioned corporate sway over research; by September the follow-up strategy named no pesticide, recommended no new limits, and pressed the case for trusting the EPA's existing review process. CropLife calls that shift "a win for farmers and the crop protection industry" and credits a campaign of farmer letters, meetings inside the administration, advertising and outreach on the Hill. Its president, Alexandra Dunn, told Brownfield News that the White House "opened their doors." Records obtained by the Center for Biological Diversity also place a CropLife contact in a meeting on the strategy with a senior EPA adviser who had lobbied for Corteva Agriscience. The group says it shares the commission's goal of getting affordable, nutritious food to children.
title: U.S. Right to Know: CropLife Claims the Weakened MAHA Strategy as Its Top 2025 Achievement

description: The Center for American Progress put out "You Are What You Eat: An Alternative to MAHA for Healthy Food and Fewer Chemicals," arguing that progressives should take back the lead on food and chemical safety from a movement whose promises it says have gone unkept. Written by CAP president Neera Tanden with Topher Spiro, Anne Knapke, Jill Rosenthal and Kierra B. Jones, it would stand up an independent Preventive Health Science Commission, charged with vaccine recommendations, preventive service recommendations and dietary guidelines, weighing the evidence on chemical safety, revisit pesticides that peer countries have already banned, and decide what food warning labels say. It would also build a National Institute of Nutrition inside the NIH to fund research on food and health that industry does not pay for; ban outright the chemicals in food and household products where the evidence of harm is already overwhelming; and invert the burden of proof, demanding fast-track reviews that affirmatively establish the safety of chemicals in food, supplements and cosmetics rather than presuming it, with parallel reviews of pesticide residue and a restored margin for children's exposure. On the consumption side it calls for front-of-pack warnings covering ultra-processed foods, fruit and vegetables for every elementary school pupil, a national healthy food incentive scheme, and parity between fruit and vegetable subsidies and those paid on other crops. Spiro's framing of the administration was blunt: it had pledged to make the country healthier and then spent two years siding with industry.
title: Center for American Progress Publishes a Rival Agenda to MAHA

description: Calley Means, a senior adviser to Health Secretary Kennedy and one of the architects of the MAHA agenda, resigned on October 22, less than two weeks before the midterms. He thanked Trump and Kennedy and said the movement is just getting started, without giving a reason. Reporting by NBC News and Politico cited sources saying he had grown frustrated at the lack of progress on his priorities. NBC's source named the administration's failure to release a federal definition of ultra-processed foods, which was teased in August, as the final straw, and also pointed to Trump's executive order boosting glyphosate supply and EPA actions that clashed with Kennedy's agenda. Bloomberg noted that big food companies had fought his push for the definition. His exit follows the earlier departures of FDA Commissioner Marty Makary and vaccine regulator Vinay Prasad, and it deepens the rift between grassroots MAHA activists and the White House.
title: Calley Means, Top MAHA Adviser to Kennedy, Resigns From the Administration

description: Michael Pollan published "American Sustenance" in The Atlantic, adapted from the preface to the twentieth-anniversary edition of The Omnivore's Dilemma, issued by Penguin Press the same day. He traces MAHA back to the customers he met at Joel Salatin's libertarian Polyface Farm: young mothers anxious about their children's health, many of them homeschoolers and homesteaders, "people who have already opted out once," as Salatin puts it. Their convictions about food ran strong and sometimes ahead of the evidence, with seed oils and grains treated as harms, raw milk as a remedy and "clean" eating as medicine. Salatin has since become a MAHA figure consulted by administration officials, and told Pollan he was approached during the transition about running the USDA. Pollan describes the movement as libertarian at its core and more concerned with individual than environmental health, quoting Marion Nestle's view that it leaves "everything up to the individual with little attention to policy." He cites MAHA activists working with Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-ME) to strip pesticide-liability protection from an appropriations bill as early evidence of a cross-party coalition.
title: Michael Pollan Weighs MAHA in His Twentieth-Anniversary Essay on The Omnivore's Dilemma

title: Kennedy Announces $11 Million in Rural Health Funding for New Hampshire

description: Rural hospitals are closing labor and delivery units, and some cite the Medicaid cuts. Vaishu Jawahar of Protect Our Care called the cuts the nail in the coffin for many units. The article does not mention MAHA; the connection here is the shared reconciliation law.
title: The New Republic Links Rural Maternity Closures to the Medicaid Cuts

description: ABC News reported that more than 200 MAHA activists sent Trump an open letter warning that the glyphosate issue could cost Republicans their House majority. Democrats, including Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, are courting disaffected MAHA voters. Note: Axios reported a letter from 241 MAHA activists in August 2025 carrying the same warning about the House majority, so this October coverage may describe that earlier letter rather than a new one.
title: 200+ MAHA Activists Warn Glyphosate Could Cost Republicans the House

title: MAHA Action's Tony Lyons Urges Unity Before the Midterms

description: California's Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment announced its intent to add atrazine to the Proposition 65 cancer list, based on IARC's Group 2A classification. The listing would require warnings rather than a ban; atrazine has been listed as a reproductive toxicant since 2016. Public comments are open until November 9, 2026. EPA dismissed the IARC classification last year. This is a proposed listing, not a final action.
title: California Moves to List Atrazine as a Carcinogen Under Proposition 65

title: Kennedy's AI Push Splits MAHA Allies

title: GAO Issues First Review of the Rural Health Transformation Program

Kennedy said AI would free Americans from medical tyranny, while activists including Robert Malone and Mary Talley Bowden condemned the corporate sponsorship.
title: MAHA Summit in Washington Draws Corporate Sponsors and Internal Criticism

description: The order directs a campaign to cut Washington D.C.'s invasive mosquito population by 90 percent and ticks by 50 percent by 2028 using non-chemical and technology-enabled methods. It also directs EPA to draft a release framework that must consider safe genetic modification, and names alpha-gal syndrome for an HHS research agenda.
title: Executive Order 14433 Targets Ticks and Mosquitoes with Non-Chemical Methods

description: Three women with non-Hodgkin lymphoma who are outside the settlement are suing on design-defect and testing claims that the Supreme Court did not directly address. Their lawyer told jurors that EPA approval of Roundup does not mean it is safe. The case is an early test of what survives Durnell.
title: First Roundup Trial Since Durnell Begins on Design-Defect Claims

description: The New York Times reported that Kennedy's financial disclosure showed $4 million in book advances from Tony Lyons' Skyhorse Publishing and more than $270,000 in gifts. His wife, Cheryl Hines, received $210,000 in consulting fees from MAHA Action. Ethics experts said the arrangements may violate federal rules; HHS says Kennedy complies with all of them.

description: The two agencies agreed to share science and expand research on glyphosate's health effects, while EPA retained sole authority over registration. Zeldin said reexamining pesticides against current science is exactly what the agency is doing with glyphosate. EPA now expects to complete its human health risk assessment in early 2027, a slip from the previously promised year-end timeline.
title: EPA and HHS Sign a Glyphosate Research Agreement

description: CNN reported that the CDC had issued no Covid-19 vaccine recommendations for the season because its advisory panel had been in disarray since March, when a judge blocked an HHS overhaul of the immunization schedule. The AP added that the CDC kept the prior year's flu endorsements, citing legal uncertainties and inquiries.
title: CDC Vaccine Recommendations Stall Amid Advisory Panel Disarray

HHS said its officials did not plan the summit and were unaware of the arrangements.
title: Bloomberg Reports Paid Access at the MAHA Summit

description: A Missouri judge heard objections to Bayer's $7.25 billion class settlement and did not rule from the bench. Monsanto's lawyer told the court there is not another settlement, and the company maintains the deal is fair to all parties and warrants final approval. As of early October no decision had been issued.
title: Roundup Settlement Gets Its Fairness Hearing

description: The Cost of Living Healthcare Working Group, which Hakeem Jeffries convened in June as one of five such panels, sent the House Democratic leader an 84-page health agenda dated September 1, assembled from 93 meetings with 139 members and 145 outside organisations and co-led by Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Terri Sewell. Its seventh section is titled "Reclaiming MAHA and Protecting American Families," an open bid for the food and chemical politics the movement has had to itself. First among the bills it would move in the opening hundred hours is the No Immunity for Glyphosate Act, carried by Thomas Massie and Chellie Pingree, which would strip funding from Trump's glyphosate executive order and keep state-law claims against Bayer and Monsanto alive; alongside it sits Rosa DeLauro's infant formula bill, requiring pathogen testing of both plants and finished product. Within a hundred days it would take up Frank Pallone's GRAS Act, ending the self-certification that lets manufacturers rule their own additives safe, which the memo calls the largest gap in American food safety law. Further out are Jim McGovern's bill banning paraquat, organophosphates and neonicotinoids, limits on PFAS in food packaging, and a ban on synthetic dyes in federal school meals. The wider agenda also presses to keep vaccine advice clear of political interference and to release withheld NIH money. Ocasio-Cortez has spent months in meetings with MAHA grassroots leaders, where pesticides and PFAS are common ground and vaccines are not. The movement's own leadership was unimpressed: Tony Lyons, who runs its political committee, said in September that "She is not our ally," though he later allowed it should work with anyone sharing its goals.

sources.label: Marler Blog analysis of the food chapter
Politico Playbook: inside AOC's MAHA outreach

title: AOC and Sewell's Working Group Puts "Reclaiming MAHA" in Writing

description: Republicans voted down Booker's amendment along party lines, and Chairman John Boozman recessed the committee indefinitely. Booker said the Durnell ruling had wiped out tens of thousands of active court cases, and argued his amendment would have restored the fundamental right of cancer victims to have their day in court.
title: Senate Agriculture Committee Rejects Booker's Liability Amendment on a Party-Line Vote

description: The last manufacturer cancelled its California paraquat registration on August 6, and the Department of Pesticide Regulation announced a statewide phase-out on August 10. Manufacturers withdrew rather than submit safety data DPR had demanded by June 5, after its review flagged thyroid harm, birth defects, and risks to birds. This is a phase-out rather than an outright ban: existing stock may be sold and used for up to two years. California uses more paraquat than any other state.
title: California Begins Phasing Out Paraquat as Manufacturers Withdraw

description: In a single week Kennedy campaigned in Danville, Virginia; Goldsboro, North Carolina; Nashville; Lexington, Kentucky; and Atlanta, promoting the administration's MAHA record. Some MAHA voters remained frustrated over glyphosate and childhood vaccines, and MAHA PAC has fallen far short of its $100 million fundraising pledge.
title: Kennedy Campaigns Across Five Southern States Ahead of the Midterms

description: With failure-to-warn claims blocked by Durnell, Bayer's proposed $7.25 billion class settlement became the principal route for resolving remaining Roundup cases. The ruling is expected to end most other litigation over the product.
title: Bayer's $7.25 Billion Settlement Becomes the Center of Roundup Litigation

description: A CDC study found that nearly a quarter of adults in states with established lone star tick populations carry alpha-gal antibodies, which indicate past exposure rather than confirmed allergy. By July 22 Kennedy was telling reporters he takes the explosion of alpha-gal seriously, though Roll Call noted that he has overstated the scale of the problem.
title: CDC Study Puts Alpha-Gal, the Tick-Borne Red Meat Allergy, on the MAHA Agenda

description: The week after the Durnell ruling, the administration promoted its regenerative agriculture pilot program as a gesture toward MAHA, without expanding its funding. Critics including Marion Nestle noted that the program's working definition of regenerative agriculture still permits glyphosate use.
title: Administration Promotes Regenerative Agriculture Pilot Without New Funding

description: EPA said it would host a summer roundtable on paraquat, a weedkiller linked to Parkinson's disease, and ordered manufacturers to conduct a real-world field volatility study. Later reporting by The New Lede found that as of autumn 2026 no such roundtable had been held or scheduled. Separately, Syngenta had said in March that it would stop selling paraquat products by the end of June.
title: EPA Announces Paraquat Roundtable and Orders Field Volatility Study

description: Senator Cory Booker said he would lead an amendment to strip away the preemptive authority the Court had affirmed, and Representative Anna Paulina Luna said she would introduce a bill removing pesticide manufacturers' liability protections. MAHA leader Vani Hari called the ruling one of the most consequential moments for corporate accountability in a generation. Both measures were proposals, not enacted law.
title: Booker and Luna Move to Undo the Liability Shield

description: In Monsanto v. Durnell the Court held 7-2 that federal pesticide law preempts state-law claims that Roundup required a cancer warning. Justice Kavanaugh wrote for the majority; Justices Jackson and Gorsuch dissented. The decision threw out a $1.25 million Missouri verdict won by John Durnell, who attributed his non-Hodgkin lymphoma to Roundup. The Trump administration had argued on Bayer's side. Bayer shares closed up nearly 19 percent, their largest single-day gain since 2003.
title: Supreme Court Rules for Monsanto in Durnell, Shielding Pesticide Makers from State Failure-to-Warn Claims

description: Prominent MAHA figures including Kelly Ryerson ('Glyphosate Girl') said the decision cost the administration the movement's loyalty. Senator Cory Booker promised a farm bill amendment to undo the liability shield, and activists directed blame at EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin.
title: MAHA Activists Call the Durnell Ruling a Betrayal

description: Zach Lahn, a businessman and farmer who was unknown in Iowa politics before entering the race in November, won the Republican nomination for governor over Rep. Randy Feenstra, whom Trump had endorsed and called "MAGA all the way" the week before the vote. Lahn ran at the agrichemical industry from the right. He wants pesticide manufacturers stripped of their liability shields, backs regenerative farming, and promised to "take on the big ag cartels. I will break up their monopolies, and I will get Iowa farmers a fair deal." He put the state's cancer rate at the center of the campaign, asserting that Iowa has "the fastest growing cancer rate in the world," a claim the Associated Press reported without corroborating. He dismissed water treatment upgrades as a Band-Aid, arguing the aim should be cutting the nitrate load before it reaches the system. MAHA PAC, run by Kennedy's publisher Tony Lyons, endorsed him, as did Turning Point Action; STAT later put spending on his behalf by MAHA-aligned PACs at more than $1.5 million, part of which Lyons had announced himself: opening his podcast on September 16 he said MAHA Action PAC was giving Lahn's campaign $1 million that week, "because we believe that regenerative farming, freedom and family values are the way to restore our nation's health." On the Supreme Court's Roundup decision he was blunt: "This will not go on when I'm governor." Trump endorsed Lahn once the primary was settled and went to Iowa to campaign for him.
title: MAHA-Backed Zach Lahn Upsets Trump's Pick in the Iowa Governor Primary

description: The back-and-forth between establishment psychiatrists, moderately critical clinicians (who often remain dismissive of patient advocates), and patient advocates and reform-oriented psychiatrists has been generating a lot of noise. But the positions are getting sharper. A widely-circulated thread by @samhall404, written from a reform perspective that accepts psychiatry's legitimate benefits, identifies ten ironies in the field that, once seen, are difficult to unsee. Three stand out. First, on who counts as extreme: the voices once labeled fringe anti-psychiatry were, the thread argues, "mostly patients bearing the brunt of iatrogenic harm" with lived experience and mounting evidence behind them — while those reflexively defending an outdated "safe and effective" paradigm have become the ideological extremists, and are "anti-patient." Second, on the deprescribing turn: the clinicians who spent years dismissing withdrawal and pathologizing patients who reported it are now rebranding as pioneers of deprescribing — "the very architects and defenders of the problem rebranding themselves as its enlightened reformers." Third, on institutional self-awareness: a field that uses "insight" and "denial" as diagnostic categories displays, the thread observes, "profound institutional denial regarding the scale of iatrogenic harm and the limitations of its core disease model."
title: The Psychiatry Debate Sharpens: Ten Ironies That Are Hard to Ignore

description: Iowa's HF 2676 was signed on May 20. Per HHS, the law limits SNAP to healthy foods; it also allows over-the-counter sale of ivermectin. The available sources do not state that it was adopted in order to earn Rural Health Transformation Program points.
title: Iowa Signs HF 2676, Limiting SNAP to 'Healthy Foods' and Allowing OTC Ivermectin

description: The New Lede — which collaborated with The Guardian in 2022–23 to publish internal Syngenta documents showing the company spent decades suppressing independent research and manipulating regulatory processes around paraquat — covered Vermont's passage of H. 739 with that backstory foregrounded. Paraquat has been used in the U.S. since 1964 and remains among the country's most widely used herbicides despite being banned in the EU and dozens of other nations. NIH studies link it to substantially elevated Parkinson's risk; research also connects it to non-Hodgkin lymphoma and childhood leukemia. Parkinson's cases have doubled globally in 25 years. In March 2026, Syngenta announced it would cease production, though generic versions remain available. Rep. Michelle Bos-Lun, a bill sponsor, said: "We have to do something to phase this out. Our job is to support farmers."
title: Vermont's Paraquat Ban and the Decades of Corporate Suppression Behind It

description: The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service released a review concluding that atrazine, a herbicide applied to roughly 75 million acres of American crops each year, does not pose an extinction risk to threatened or endangered species. The finding reverses a 2021 EPA determination, reached after a court-ordered review, that atrazine was likely to harm more than 1,000 protected species. Atrazine has been banned by the EU since the early 2000s and restricted by at least three dozen other countries. In 2025 the WHO classified it as probably carcinogenic to humans; it has also been linked to hormonal disruption in amphibians, birth defects, and waterway contamination. The primary manufacturer is Syngenta, owned by the Chinese conglomerate Sinochem. The outcome was a win for the Farm Bureau and the National Corn Growers Association, which argued that restrictions would cut crop yields and raise food costs. It landed as a direct rebuke to MAHA. Nathan Donley of the Center for Biological Diversity, whose lawsuit triggered the review, said: "This is the most widespread pesticide water contaminant in the United States. It's an absolute joke to think that these mitigations are going to prevent serious harm to species that are on the brink of extinction." Vani Hari, a healthy-eating activist who has advised the Trump administration on food policy, was pointed: "The public is watching a government that moves faster to protect chemical companies than it does to protect children, farmers, wildlife, or drinking water. That is exactly why so many Americans believe regulatory agencies have been captured by corporate interests."
title: Fish and Wildlife Service Clears Atrazine, Splitting MAHA from the Administration It Helped Elect

description: The Senate confirmed former New Mexico Rep. Steve Pearce as Director of the Bureau of Land Management along party lines. Environmental groups raised alarm over Pearce's record of opposition to national parks and forests. The BLM oversees 245 million acres of public land nationally, including 15 million in California alone. Colin Barrows of the CactusToCloud Institute called the appointment "the fox running the henhouse."
title: Senate Confirms Steve Pearce as BLM Director Over Environmentalists' Objections

description: Montana's SNAP restriction waiver was approved on May 19, one of the eight policy actions CMS scored in the Rural Health Transformation Program. The available sources do not state that it was adopted in order to earn program points.
title: Montana SNAP Restriction Waiver Approved

description: Vermont's legislature passed H. 739, making it the first U.S. state to ban paraquat, an herbicide that more than 70 countries — including every EU member and China — have already prohibited. Exposure to paraquat roughly doubles the risk of Parkinson's disease compared to other pesticides. The bill awaits Gov. Phil Scott's signature and phases in a full statewide ban by December 2030, giving farmers transition time and encouraging adoption of safer alternatives. The Michael J. Fox Foundation applauded the vote and called on other states and the federal government to follow. Dan Feehan of the Foundation said: "The evidence linking paraquat exposure to increased Parkinson's risk is strong and has been building for decades." Similar bills are pending in a dozen states including New York, Pennsylvania, and Minnesota.
title: H. 739 — First U.S. Ban on Paraquat

description: Laura Delano, a public advocate and author who has written extensively about her own psychiatric drug withdrawal, posted a detailed response on X to the NYT Well piece on stopping antidepressants. She commended the Times for covering tapering guidance but challenged five specific claims. The safety characterization rests on clinical trials that typically last six to eight weeks, not the years or decades millions of people are prescribed these drugs. The advice to wait until a patient feels stable before stopping may keep people on medications they are not benefiting from. And the relapse statistics in the piece are compromised at their source: withdrawal symptoms are "routinely misclassified as relapse," she wrote, making it nearly impossible to determine who actually has a chronic condition that warrants indefinite medication use. Her sharpest challenge was to the tapering protocol. The 25-percent-per-week guideline presented as standard clinical practice is, she argued, "essentially cold turkey, and incredibly dangerous" for many patients. Because physicians have not been trained in hyperbolic tapering methods, what clinical settings consider a slow taper can trigger symptoms lasting months or years, which are then misread as relapse. Withdrawal is not merely "uncomfortable," as the article frames it, but can be "life-altering," she wrote, in some cases causing people to 'lose the ability to work or care for themselves or their families, end up hospitalized, or sometimes even kill themselves out of desperation for relief from the pain.'In a separate post, she offered a pointed clarification: "Advocating that people who want to stop their antidepressants are provided with safe, reliable information about tapering off them is not the same thing as advocating that people taper off antidepressants." The distinction matters because critics of the withdrawal advocacy movement routinely conflate the two, treating any push for better discontinuation guidance as covert anti-medication activism.
title: Laura Delano Responds to the NYT Well Antidepressant Tapering Piece

description: The EPA formally proposed repealing drinking water limits for four PFAS compounds and giving utilities more time to comply with limits on two others, unraveling the first new national drinking water standard the agency had successfully set since 1996. The Biden rules, finalized in 2024, were estimated to reduce PFAS exposure for roughly 100 million people. All 50 states have recorded PFAS levels above those standards. The administration's rationale is procedural: EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin argued the rules were procedurally flawed, contending the Biden EPA had moved too quickly and left them legally vulnerable to challenge. The two most studied compounds, PFOS and PFOA, will retain their limits, though utilities can apply for a two-year compliance extension. "The science on these two chemicals is some of the strongest on any drinking water contaminant we regulate," Zeldin said. "Those levels are staying." Environmental groups are skeptical even of that concession. The Environmental Working Group and the NRDC argue the rollback likely violates the Safe Drinking Water Act's anti-backsliding provision, which bars the agency from weakening standards once set, and that the extended compliance timeline for PFOS and PFOA may itself run afoul of the law's five-year implementation requirement. The move drew open criticism from within the MAHA coalition, a notable fracture. Conservative wellness influencer and MAHA ally Alex Clark said: "I am tired of making excuses for dangerous chemicals to continue flooding our environment and harming our kids." David Andrews, chief science officer at the Environmental Working Group, was direct: "I don't see how you put a positive light on this. Ultimately, I see this as a betrayal of public health and the mission of making America healthier." Kennedy, who appeared alongside Zeldin at the announcement, highlighted HHS research efforts on PFAS destruction technology but did not defend the rollback directly. When pressed at a congressional hearing in April about EPA actions that appeared to contradict MAHA, he told lawmakers it fell outside his department's purview.
title: EPA Moves to Repeal Biden PFAS Drinking Water Limits, Drawing Criticism from MAHA Allies

description: Awais Aftab, a psychiatrist who writes at Psychiatry at the Margins, published a pointed response to the Bergner NYT Magazine piece arguing that it obscures what is actually driving the MAHA psychiatric agenda. Bergner frames the movement as a corrective to 1980s reductive psychiatry, but Aftab contends this construction flattens a much larger middle ground: George Engel had already articulated the biopsychosocial model in 1980 alongside the supposed medical model takeover, and most mainstream psychiatry has long operated somewhere between the extremes Bergner describes. The deeper problem, he argues, is that Bergner treats Thomas Szasz as a fringe figure when Szaszian ideas are in fact "load-bearing" for the movement. The core claim is that mental illness is a life reaction rather than a biological disorder. In MAHA-adjacent spaces this gets presented through the moderate language of overprescribing and overmedicalization, but the underlying agenda would not survive scrutiny if stated plainly. Aftab is unsparing about the Whitaker-Moncrieff framework: "the Whitaker-Moncrieff version of critical psychiatry, at its core, is a philosophically and scientifically exhausted movement" — unable to persuade clinical communities through evidence, he argues, and now pivoting toward political channels instead. He acknowledges real gaps in clinical guidance on antidepressant discontinuation. But on the broader MAHA psychiatric project, he is unsparing, arguing the movement represents "the health rhetoric of twenty-first-century American fascism" and endangers evidence-based care and public health infrastructure.We want to register a methodological critique of Aftab's framing here. In our own research on the psychiatric survivor movement ("The Politics of Rationality: Psychiatric Survivors' Challenge to Psychiatry," in Tactical Biopolitics, MIT Press, 2008), we traced a history far more complex than a Szaszian core: the movement emerged from the radical milieu of the 1970s, fractured under 1980s neoliberalism as a consumer advocacy strand was absorbed into the pharmaceutical-funded mainstream, and reconstituted in the 1990s around harm reduction and Internet-enabled organizing. That research also showed that the movement's more radical figures have demanded better science and epistemic accountability from psychiatry. A 2003 hunger strike organized by survivors forced the American Psychiatric Association to acknowledge publicly that brain science had not advanced to the point of identifying reliable biomarkers for mental illness — holding an institution to its own stated standards. And on the question of medication, the movement's own framing has long been explicitly pro-choice and harm-reduction oriented. As The Freedom Center's co-founder put it in an interview quoted in the chapter: "pro-choice is a way to deal with the reality of individuals on medications who feel judged and alienated. We don't want to be shrinks in reverse. We are a harm reduction movement — we are not advocating abstinence and we respect that people make difficult decisions." The deeper point is this: Aftab's argument demands evidentiary rigor from psychiatry's critics while making its own social-scientific claims about what drives the movement and what its philosophical core really is without equivalent grounding. If we are going to make strong claims about a social movement, we need to base them on research into that movement, not on inference from observed patterns. That said, his concern about the MAHA alliance is real. The movement has faced and survived co-optation before, most visibly when neoliberal consumer frameworks nearly swallowed its politics in the 1980s. The current entanglement with a government many analysts describe as authoritarian or fascist is a more dangerous version of that dynamic. Working within that coalition, and lending it credibility, can reasonably be read as tacit support for something fascist in its tendency. But motivations in the current alliance are mixed: some figures appear ideologically aligned; others are riding a moment of unusual political attention to amplify work that has long been ignored. Whether that is complicity or opportunism is a real question, and one that inference alone cannot answer.
title: Psychiatry at the Margins: Does MAHA Have a Szaszian Heart? A Strong Claim That Fails to Stand Given Lack of Empirical Back up

description: Daniel Bergner, writing for the NYT Magazine, gives the critical psychiatry movement the most serious intellectual treatment it has received in mainstream coverage of the Kennedy era. Rather than framing the May 4 summit as a political stunt or a MAHA curiosity, Bergner traces the decades-long intellectual genealogy of reform — from the 1980 DSM overhaul that anchored psychiatry to a medical model it was never quite able to prove, through Prozac's promise of effortless recalibration, to the accumulating doubts about whether the chemical imbalance theory that sold the drugs was ever more than a marketing frame. That history is what gives the reform movement its substance, and Bergner treats it as such. The piece centers on Laura Delano and her husband Cooper Davis as the movement's most strategically positioned figures: former psychiatric patient turned activist, now shaping HHS training materials and helping design summit policy documents. Their politics do not map neatly onto the Trump coalition — Delano describes her outlook as "critiquing unchecked, unjust power" — but they have concluded the administration is the most plausible lever for the change they want. The piece is candid about the tensions this creates. Robert Whitaker, whose book Delano credits with redirecting her life, is skeptical that "overmedicalization" framing goes far enough: "I don't think serious reform is enough," he told Bergner. Others in the movement fear the MAHA association taints them as anti-science by proximity to the anti-vax contingent. Awais Aftab, a clinical associate professor at Case Western Reserve who sits closer to the mainstream than most critics, supplied perhaps the piece's sharpest line: "for decades, mainstream psychiatry willfully blinded itself to the burden and severity of withdrawal and discontinuation-related difficulties from antidepressants and other psychiatric medications." Bergner notes two concrete policy outcomes already in motion: CMS will reimburse clinicians for time spent helping patients taper, and HHS will distribute deprescribing training to thousands of practitioners with Delano as a presenter. Whether these gains lead anywhere approaching the transformation the movement envisions is another question. Bergner is clear about what stands in the way: a pharmaceutical industry with the resources to run psychotropic drug ads through every commercial break, and an establishment that has spent fifty years building its authority on the medical model it would now have to abandon.
title: NYT Magazine: The Critical Psychiatry Movement That Found an Unlikely Ally in the Trump Administration

description: A Washington Post opinion piece framed Makary's forced exit as "a much-needed opportunity to reset" the FDA, urging a "more constructive relationship with medical innovators" and warning the next commissioner to "tread carefully when telling Americans what they can eat." On youth vaping, the piece dismissed child health concerns by claiming Makary's resistance to flavored e-cigarette approvals reflected "heavy-handed bans" that "only created a more dangerous black market" — a standard tobacco industry argument that research does not support; flavor restrictions consistently reduce youth use. Food and agriculture journalist Helena Bottemiller Evich called the piece "truly baffling," noting the factual premise that FDA needed reining in was unfounded: "FDA has not issued a single new food regulation during this administration. FDA has not banned a single food chemical during this administration. FDA has not banned a single food product during this administration."
title: WaPo Editorial Reframes Makary's Firing as Deregulatory Opportunity, Amplifying Industry Talking Points

description: Reporter Ariana Eunjung Cha offers something the May 2026 SSRI debate has mostly lacked: a piece that takes seriously both the value these medications have for millions of people (Cha notes that SSRIs help millions "regain stability") and the patient experience of discontinuation that the medical establishment spent years minimizing. The science shows that experiences coming off them vary widely. Cha's piece centers on those for whom stopping proved far harder than they were ever told it would be, and on how that difficulty was explained away rather than studied. Drug companies for years characterized discontinuation symptoms as typically mild and brief, and rebranded the phenomenon as something other than withdrawal, what researcher Mark Horowitz calls "industry euphemisms." The clinical reality for some patients was quite different, and it went largely undocumented because nobody was looking. Horowitz turned to the research after his own experience stopping SSRIs in his early 20s: "my life kind of exploded," he told the Post. "I was trapped on the drug." What he found was a pharmacological explanation for why some patients struggle most at the very end of a taper, when clinicians and patients alike assume the worst is behind them. His 2019 paper in Lancet Psychiatry on this dose-response dynamic drove a revision of UK clinical guidelines; US guidance has barely moved. Yale psychiatrist Gerard Sanacora identifies a separate systemic failure in the system's approach to renewals: stable patients get automatic refills, with no mechanism built in for reassessing whether the prescription is still needed. Stable patients get automatic renewals, and the therapy alternatives that might make medication unnecessary are costlier and harder to access. "It's really not so much an issue of overuse," Sanacora told Cha. "It's an issue of appropriate and inappropriate use." Patient Michael Bosco, 36, on antidepressants since age 8, tried twice to stop under standard medical advice before finding Horowitz's slower protocol. "I don't think people understand you don't have a life if you do it the wrong way," he said. Awais Aftab of Case Western Reserve names the trap Kennedy has now sprung: "the gap in scientific knowledge has allowed a kind of polarized discourse. Some people dismiss them, and others try to exaggerate them, turning them into a panic." The piece does not say Kennedy is wrong that discontinuation deserves more attention. It implies, without quite stating it, that his arrival has turned a real but manageable clinical gap into a political flashpoint, which is the last thing patients navigating a difficult taper actually need.
title: Washington Post: The Long-Ignored Science of SSRI Withdrawal, Now Caught in Kennedy's Political War

description: Dana G. Smith's practical piece for the NYT Well section appeared the day Kennedy's summit dominated health coverage and reads as a quiet rebuttal to the political framing around it. Rather than debating overprescribing, Smith asked practicing psychiatrists what the clinical guidance actually says. Their answers are more cautious and individualized than anything Kennedy offered. Experts stress that SSRIs are safe drugs with few serious health risks, that the decision to stop is highly personal, and that the key factors are relapse history, life circumstances, and whether the patient feels like themselves again. The piece is useful on a specific question the policy debate has largely blurred: how to tell withdrawal from returning illness. "Depression tends to return insidiously over a period of weeks or months, whereas withdrawal symptoms come in with a bang almost immediately," said David Taylor, a professor of psychopharmacology at King's College London. And for patients who have found a medication that works, Taylor's closing note is worth keeping: "If they found a medication that allows them to have a happy life and a productive life, then with some minor exceptions and with some caution, those people probably should continue — because a relapse could be disastrous."Laura Delano, a prominent voice in the antidepressant withdrawal advocacy space, responded on X with a point-by-point critique that accepted the piece's value but challenged several of its underlying claims. She noted that the 'very safe' characterization of SSRIs rests on clinical trials typically lasting six to eight weeks, not the years or decades millions of patients take them. On tapering, she was direct: the piece's 25-percent-per-week protocol is "essentially cold turkey, and incredibly dangerous" for many patients, because the medical profession has not been trained in safe hyperbolic tapering and routinely misdiagnoses withdrawal as relapse as a result. She also challenged the relapse statistics the article cites: withdrawal symptoms are "routinely misclassified as relapse," she wrote, making it difficult to determine who actually has a chronic condition warranting indefinite medication use.
title: NYT Well: What Psychiatrists Actually Say About Stopping Antidepressants

description: Trump forced out FDA Commissioner Marty Makary on May 12 after months of friction over his resistance to approving fruit-flavored e-cigarettes and his refusal to restrict mifepristone. Trump said only that Makary "was having some difficulty," without specifying whether he fired or requested his resignation. The following day, Rich Danker, RFK Jr.'s chief HHS spokesperson, submitted his own resignation letter citing concerns about "approval of e-cigarette flavors that would appeal to children and expose them to nicotine addiction, lung damage, and higher risk of cancer." Kyle Diamantas, the FDA's deputy food commissioner, was named acting commissioner.
title: Trump Forces Out FDA Commissioner Makary; RFK Jr.'s Spokesperson Resigns in Protest

description: A New York Times investigation published May 13 documents the direct line from tobacco industry money to an FDA policy reversal. On May 3, President Trump lunched with tobacco executives and lobbyists at his Jupiter, Fla. golf club — including top officials from Reynolds American and Altria, and lobbyist Brian Ballard, a major Trump fundraiser whose firm has been paid more than $4.4 million by Reynolds since 2017. When the executives complained about FDA vaping rules, Trump interrupted to call Commissioner Makary on the spot. No answer. He then called RFK Jr. and Dr. Oz directly to register his displeasure. Less than a week later, the FDA issued guidance opening the door to flavored vape sales — bypassing the scientific review process the agency had defended up to the Supreme Court. Makary resigned rather than sign off. The donation trail is unambiguous: Reynolds gave $10 million to a Trump super PAC during the 2024 campaign and $3 million more after his win; Altria gave $1 million to the inaugural and $1 million to a super PAC; the Vapor Technology Association gave $1.25 million to the inaugural; Reynolds and Altria each donated to Trump's proposed White House ballroom fundraiser and their executives attended the $2.5 million-per-donor dinner. Trump referred to Reynolds officials as "my tobacco guys." The administration's position: "The only guiding factor behind the Trump administration's health policymaking is gold standard science."
title: Big Tobacco Buys an FDA Policy: Executives Dine with Trump, Vaping Rules Reversed Within a Week

description: The Trump EPA moved to strike down 2024 regulations on ethylene oxide (EtO), a carcinogenic gas used to sterilize 20 billion medical devices annually and linked to leukemia. Recent research found EtO is 60 times more carcinogenic than 2006 estimates; the Biden rule required a 90% emissions cut across 89 facilities. Repealing it would leave 2.3 million people, disproportionately in working-class and low-income communities, breathing nearly 8 tons of the gas each year, while saving industry $47 million annually. No accounting for the resulting cancer burden has been produced. The deeper legal problem: the administration is arguing the Clean Air Act does not authorize discretionary risk reviews beyond the first mandatory one, permanently curtailing the EPA's ability to update protections as new science emerges. "This sends up a signal flare to everyone that we've got a real threat, and that the administration plans to gut cancer protections," said Erik Olson of the NRDC. A Harvard analysis confirms the move is "part of a broader pattern of authority-limiting interpretations by the EPA" under this administration.
title: Trump EPA Moves to Repeal EtO Cancer Protections, Curtailing Future Regulatory Authority

description: The Trump administration has shelved a 2024 MSHA rule that would have brought silica dust limits in coal mines down from 100 to 50 micrograms per cubic meter; the compliance window was due to open in April 2025. Unlike coal dust, silica particles embed in lung tissue and trigger irreversible scarring with no treatment. The condition now hits 1 in 10 miners with 25 or more years underground and is reaching workers in their 30s and 40s. MSHA's workforce has simultaneously contracted, with 90 newly hired inspectors losing their positions. This comes as the administration signed an executive order naming coal a national security priority. "If the Trump administration actually cared about protecting coal miners from black lung, we'd have a strong silica rule in place right now," said Rebecca Shelton of the Appalachian Citizens' Law Center. "Instead, they are hiding behind a ridiculous legal process to delay action while miners get sick and die."
title: Trump Administration Shelves Black Lung Silica Rule as Miners Get Sick and Die

description: A CNN report documents the widening rift between the MAHA movement and the Trump White House, centered on the collapse of Casey Means's surgeon general nomination. When Trump picked Means in May 2025, he said he was deferring entirely to Kennedy: 'Bobby really thought she was great. I don't know her. I listened to the recommendation of Bobby.' Nearly a year later, after Means's candidacy stalled, Trump pulled her nomination and replaced her with Nicole Saphier, a radiologist and Fox News contributor who has no real ties to Kennedy and has repeatedly criticized him. CNN reports Kennedy played little role in the Saphier decision; she came up as one option among many compiled by White House officials. CNN frames it as the latest evidence that, after a year of letting Kennedy 'go wild,' Trump and his aides are 'shortening the leash' on the HHS secretary ahead of the midterms: installing conventional-background nominees at the CDC and surgeon general's office, pulling back HHS's push to overhaul vaccine policy in favor of issues with wider appeal like drug prices, and siding with agricultural corporations over Kennedy on glyphosate. The most striking line comes from an unnamed Trump adviser, who questioned whether the movement was ever the political force it claimed to be: 'I hate to say it, but I think they're a little bit overrated. To some extent, MAHA has always been a paper tiger.' MAHA leaders pushed back hard. Turning Point USA podcaster Alex Clark, who had personally pressed Trump on Means's confirmation at the April 9 Oval Office meeting, called Saphier's selection 'a catastrophic mistake' and said she 'gets an F when it comes to all things MAHA.' Vani Hari ('Food Babe') argued the administration should leave the post vacant rather than confirm Saphier, and warned: 'This is a fast-growing, highly energized coalition of parents, farmers, and health advocates and we're organizing in ways Washington isn't used to. Ignoring that heading into the midterms is not just wrong, it's politically shortsighted.' The White House disputed any suggestion Kennedy is being sidelined; spokesman Kush Desai said MAHA 'has been a Day One priority' and Kennedy 'continues to play a central role.' CNN notes the open question some in Trump's orbit are now asking: whether MAHA will make the compromises needed to become a durable part of the GOP coalition, or remain, as one adviser put it, a 'factional offshoot on the political fringe.' Arizona GOP strategist Barrett Marson raised the inverse risk for Republicans: 'I think the right candidate, either a Democrat or Republican, could win MAHA voters with a message that they would want to hear.'
title: CNN: MAHA-MAGA Rift Widens as Trump Replaces Kennedy's Surgeon General Pick — One Adviser Calls MAHA 'a Paper Tiger'

description: On May 5, the FDA authorized the first-ever fruit-flavored e-cigarettes for adults 21 and over, mango, blueberry, and two menthol varieties from the Los Angeles brand Glas. The Wall Street Journal reported hours before the announcement that President Trump had personally pressed FDA Commissioner Marty Makary to approve flavored vapes, fulfilling a 2024 campaign pledge made after Trump met privately with a leading vaping lobbyist. On Truth Social during the campaign, Trump wrote that he 'saved Flavored Vaping in 2019' and would 'save Vaping again.' The decision reverses years of FDA work to restrict flavored e-cigarettes: the agency had previously turned away more than 1 million fruit, candy, and dessert flavors on youth-protection grounds, and the Supreme Court unanimously backed those rejections in April 2025. The FDA's release cited new 'device access restriction' technology, which requires users to verify their identity with government-issued ID and pair the device with a smartphone via Bluetooth, as a youth-protection mitigation. Bret Koplow, acting director of FDA's Center for Tobacco Products, called the technology 'a potential game changer.' The Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids panned the decision. CEO Yolonda C. Richardson said it 'puts at risk the progress our nation has made in reducing youth e-cigarette use' and 'conflicts with overwhelming scientific evidence and the FDA's own repeated conclusions that flavors pose a substantial risk to young people.' Flavored vapes have long been documented as a primary driver of youth nicotine uptake. The move directly contradicts MAHA's stated mission of reducing chronic disease in children and curbing the targeting of young people by addictive industries, a particularly sharp contradiction given Kennedy's signature framing of corporate capture of federal health agencies.
title: FDA Approves First Fruit-Flavored Vapes for Adults 21+ — After Trump Pressed Commissioner Makary

description: In an appearance on Fox Business, a typically friendly outlet for the Trump administration, host Liz Claman asked Zeldin a direct question: 'Can you point to something where you have actually tightened regulation, to make sure that we have clean air?' Zeldin offered a generic response: 'We made some decisions that increase regulation… and obviously in our agency it's air, it's water, it's land', without naming a specific air-quality tightening. He then pivoted to water quality and claimed the administration had improved standards there. Claman pushed back in real time, noting that the administration had in fact loosened the rules governing how wastewater can be disposed of near critical waterways and pressing him on how that serves drinking water safety. Zeldin retreated to existing legal frameworks: 'This is regulated with maximum contaminate levels, and the thousands of water systems then have to come into compliance', citing the Clean Water Act and Safe Drinking Water Act rather than naming any new protective rule his EPA has issued. The exchange matters for two reasons. First, the pushback came from a network that has carried the administration's environmental messaging with little resistance: per Media Matters, Zeldin has made at least 36 cable-news appearances in his first 100 days as administrator, and 35 of them have been on Fox networks. Second, on a friendly stage, Zeldin still could not produce an air-tightening example when asked, and his water claim was contradicted within seconds by his own host. The clip lands the same week as a New Yorker exposé documenting Zeldin's systematic dismantling of the EPA's research arm and his rollbacks of rules limiting Americans' exposure to arsenic, mercury, and PM2.5 (covered separately on this timeline). Coverage: Mediaite · Media Matters.
title: Watch: Even Fox Business Now Pushes Back on Zeldin — A Sign of How Anti-EPA This EPA Has Become

description: On May 4, 2026, the Department of Health and Human Services issued a Dear Colleague Letter jointly signed by SAMHSA, CMS, HRSA, and ACF on psychiatric medication and non-pharmacological treatments. The letter and the speech announcing it tell two different stories. The letter is measured, clinical, and carefully hedged. It explicitly affirms that "psychiatric medications can play an important and, at times, essential role in treatment," noting that "for many individuals, such medications reduce symptoms, improve functioning, prevent relapse, and support recovery." It frames non-pharmacological approaches (psychotherapy, sleep, physical activity, dietary strategies) as part of "a full continuum of evidence-based mental health care," not as replacements for medication. On deprescribing, the letter is unambiguous: "Deprescribing is not synonymous with abrupt discontinuation or blanket medication reduction. Rather, it is a deliberate, individualized clinical process." Decisions, it warns, "should not be undertaken abruptly or in a manner that undermines patient trust, safety, or continuity of care." The animating principles are shared decision-making, informed consent, and individualized care. Kennedy's speech at the MAHA Institute summit framed the same announcement very differently, as a political claim that Americans are over-medicated, that SSRIs are dangerous and addictive, and that the federal government is now intervening to wean people off them. Where the letter treats medication as clinically essential for many patients, Kennedy framed the country's psychiatric prescribing as a crisis of dependency: "The United States does not just face a mental health crisis, we face a dependency crisis driven by over-medicalization" (The MAHA Report). In his prepared remarks he told the audience: "Psychiatric medications have a role in care, but we will no longer treat them as the default, we will treat them as one option, to be used when appropriate, with full transparency and with a clear path off when they are no longer needed" (The New York Times). Kennedy also revived claims well outside what the letter says, or what the evidence supports. The New York Times reported that during his confirmation hearings "Mr. Kennedy claimed, without evidence, that S.S.R.I.s were partly responsible for the rise in school shootings, and that they could be harder to quit than heroin. At Monday's event, Mr. Kennedy repeated that claim." CNN catalogued his prior assertions that psychiatric drugs may be "linked with violence and mass shootings, with serious risks to developing fetuses when women take them during pregnancy, with withdrawal worse than that from heroin, and with harms to children." The Independent likewise noted Kennedy has "linked them, without evidence, to school shootings." The summit itself went further than the letter in other ways. As the New York Times reported, speakers at the daylong event "advocated a variety of steps to address the overprescription of psychiatric medications, such as phasing out school-based mental health screenings, requiring written informed consent before starting medications and featuring prominent, cigarette-style warnings on packaging." The Times also noted that "no major medical organizations were represented at the gathering." None of those proposals appear in the letter, which does not mention violence, mass shootings, or heroin, single out SSRIs, or call for cigarette-style warnings. This gap was noted explicitly by some clinicians. Forensic and clinical psychologist Dr. Nicolas Badre, quoted in HHS's own media roundup, wrote on X: "Contrary to what many may say, it is reasonable… this letter seems reasonable, common sense, and non-alarmist to me." NPR similarly captured the disconnect, quoting Dr. Vera Feuer of the Child Mind Institute saying "Some of the recommendations [are] completely reasonable" while noting that "focusing solely on the side effects of SSRIs obscures the fact that these medications still do help millions of people." The American Psychiatric Association's response engaged primarily with Kennedy's framing rather than the letter. APA CEO Dr. Marketa Wills told the New York Times: "We may take issue with this blanket 'overprescribing' hypothesis that underpins the secretary's statements. There is probably overprescribing and underprescribing in all parts of medicine, and mental health care is no different. And there are people who still can't access care at all who need it." She welcomed Kennedy's focus on mental health and hoped to help develop deprescribing guidelines, adding: "We believe clinical care is safe and should be individualized for all patients." Some of Kennedy's allies leaned into this gap to argue the press is distorting the initiative. Laura Delano (the founder of Inner Compass and one of the summit's featured speakers, quoted in the New York Times describing the moment as a "tipping point") pushed back on the coverage on X: "To anyone believing the false headlines about antidepressant 'bans' or 'restricting access to care,' I encourage you to read what @hhs and @SecKennedy are actually setting forth to do here (which is neither of those things). We must rise above the distorting spin and focus on what's actually happening: people have not been given the information, resources and support they need, and our government is finally acknowledging this and responding accordingly." Delano also shared a video clip from Kennedy's remarks at the same MAHA Institute summit: "If you are taking psychiatric medication, we're not telling you to stop. We're making sure that you and your clinician have the information and support to make the right decisions for you. That includes a safe, evidence-based path to tapering and discontinuation when clinically appropriate." The clip is from the same MAHA Institute summit speech at which Kennedy repeated his claims linking psychiatric drugs to school shootings and comparing SSRI withdrawal to heroin, but those claims do not appear in what Delano shared. The gap runs in both directions: the New York Times foregrounded Kennedy's inflammatory rhetoric without including the measured clip; Delano circulated the measured clip without the inflammatory rhetoric from the same speech. Neither account was complete. Delano is partly right that most press coverage skipped over what the letter itself actually says. But "read what HHS and Kennedy are actually setting forth to do" treats the letter and Kennedy's rhetoric as a single coherent package, when they aren't. The letter says one thing — get informed consent, individualize care, taper carefully. Kennedy said another at the same podium: Americans face a "dependency crisis," SSRIs may drive school shootings, withdrawal is worse than heroin. Which version clinicians, payers, and states ultimately operationalize will depend less on the speech than on the letter, but the letter received far less scrutiny in press coverage than the rhetoric surrounding it.
title: The MAHA Mental Health Announcement: What the Letter Said, What Kennedy Said, and What Each Side Left Out

description: Nebraska became the first state to implement Medicaid work requirements under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act on May 1, eight months before the federal deadline. The rule requires adults 19 to 64 in Medicaid expansion to document 80 hours per month of work, training, or community service. The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities estimates between 28,000 and 41,000 Nebraskans face potential coverage loss, mostly from paperwork barriers rather than failure to meet requirements. Georgetown's Center for Children and Families found that even with Nebraska's lenient self-declaration approach, roughly 28,000 people will lose coverage from bureaucratic burden alone. Governor Jim Pillen described the requirement as "a hand up, not a handout," but Sara Maresh of Nebraska Appleseed was direct: "A vast majority of Nebraskans are working or would meet an exemption. It is the red tape that's what causes the problems."
title: Nebraska Becomes First State to Implement Medicaid Work Requirements, Putting Tens of Thousands at Risk

description: A yearlong Mother Jones investigation by Nate Halverson, with data reporting by Melissa Lewis, documents that the US Forest Service and private timber companies are spraying record amounts of glyphosate (the weedkiller sold as Roundup) across California's logged and fire-damaged forests, and that the government's safety justification rests on research the manufacturer secretly shaped. Reviewing more than 5 million state pesticide records, the reporters found that glyphosate applied to California forests reached 266,000 pounds in 2023, almost five times the amount of two decades earlier, with forest application now the fastest-growing use of the chemical in the state. The Forest Service plans to spray roughly 10,000 acres of Lassen National Forest starting in spring 2026, plus up to 75,000 more acres burned in the 2021 Caldor Fire, including near Lake Tahoe ski resorts, campgrounds, and trailheads. The investigation's central revelation concerns the science behind those approvals. Internal Monsanto emails obtained through litigation show the company secretly commissioned, financed, and in some cases wrote studies that declared glyphosate safe. Among them was a 2000 review paper, lead-authored by Dr. Gary Williams, that concluded 'there is no potential for Roundup herbicide to pose a health risk to humans' while relying entirely on Monsanto's own internal data. The Forest Service's 2011 risk assessment cites that single paper 27 times, more than any other source; five of its seven most-cited articles were either orchestrated by Monsanto or written by authors with financial ties to it. In December the journal Regulatory Toxicology and Pharmacology retracted the Williams paper, saying it had 'lost confidence in the results and conclusions.' The retraction was prompted by a critical analysis from Naomi Oreskes, co-author of the 2010 book 'Merchants of Doubt' on how corporations distort science to shape policy, and Alexander Kaurov. Oreskes's framing is the heart of the piece: 'We're not claiming that this paper being retracted proves that glyphosate is scary dangerous,' she tells Mother Jones. 'We're saying it proves that Monsanto poisoned the well of public understanding of science.' Regulators, she argues, made 'a good-faith assumption that because this paper was published in a respectable, peer-reviewed journal that it was a legitimate paper,' but 'what we've shown is that it was not a legitimate paper,' rather a ploy 'to manipulate the scientific conversation and thereby the regulatory conversation.' 'As a person who studies scientific integrity, that profoundly offends me,' she says, 'but also, it's crucial because it means we can't trust what they say.' The piece lands squarely on MAHA's central fault line: Trump's coalition pairs a Big Agriculture wing dependent on glyphosate with a MAHA wing that loathes it. A 2020 EPA report found glyphosate harms 93% of endangered species, and in 2022 the 9th Circuit overturned the EPA's glyphosate safety assessment for inadequately weighing cancer risk. Yet Trump's February executive order declared the herbicide critical to national security, invoked the Defense Production Act to expand its production, and moved to shield manufacturers from lawsuits. The administration has simultaneously frozen NIH grants funding independent glyphosate research, leaving long-running studies such as UC Berkeley researcher Brenda Eskenazi's at risk of shutting down.
title: Mother Jones Investigation: Record Glyphosate Spraying on California Forests, Built on Safety Science Monsanto 'Poisoned'

description: In 12 states with available data, more than 700,000 children have lost SNAP food assistance since H.R. 1 passed in July 2025. Nutrition is the foundation of the health outcomes MAHA says it wants: SNAP is linked to better birth outcomes, lower childhood disease rates, and higher adult earnings — CBPP estimates every dollar invested returns $62 in lifetime value. The law shifts benefit costs to states based on their payment error rate, incentivizing paperwork barriers over fixes. Arizona lost 200,000 child participants; 81 percent of calls to Massachusetts SNAP caseworkers were disconnected by March. Children who fall off SNAP also lose access to WIC and free school meals. The movement cannot credibly claim to put children's health first while the administration it helped elect strips away the food assistance that makes that health possible.
title: You Can't MAHA Without Food: 700,000 Children Have Lost SNAP Since H.R. 1

description: State auditor Rob Sand, the Democratic nominee for governor, released a health and water plan built around Iowa's cancer rate. It would create a cancer task force inside the state's Department of Health and Human Services, restore funding for the Iowa Water Quality Information System that the legislature defunded in 2023, alert Iowans when nitrate levels in drinking water pass the federal limit, open livestock operations' manure management records to the public, and expand radon testing, which Sand wants home inspectors to raise with prospective buyers. For farmers the plan offers incentives rather than rules: an income tax credit toward conservation practices and a property tax break for farms that follow approved nutrient plans. On the chemical industry he was direct — "We shouldn't be doing immunity for chemical companies that are sickening Iowans" — a reference to the Bayer-backed bill the Iowa Senate passed to block failure-to-warn suits over federally labeled products. He also pointed out that a key study clearing Roundup's active ingredient had since been withdrawn by the journal that ran it. Asked whether he would put new regulations on farms, he did not rule it out, saying he believes in "enforcement for everything."
title: Rob Sand Runs for Iowa Governor on a Cancer Task Force and the State's Water

description: On the morning of April 30, the House passed an amendment 280–142 to strip pesticide-labeling language from the 2026 farm bill, a MAHA-priority outcome that hinged on overwhelming Democratic support. The party breakdowns tell the story. Among Democrats: 207 voted yes, only 6 voted no, near-unanimous support for stripping the liability shield. Among Republicans, the picture flipped: 73 voted yes (the MAHA-aligned faction) and 136 voted no, meaning the MAHA wing was outvoted nearly two-to-one inside its own caucus. The amendment cleared the chamber only because the Democratic 'yes' bloc more than tripled the size of the Republican 'yes' bloc. Without that essential Democratic support, the MAHA-led effort would have failed. The six Democratic defectors who voted to preserve the shield were Sanford Bishop (Ga.), Henry Cuellar (Texas), Don Davis (N.C.), Vicente Gonzalez (Texas), Adam Gray (Calif.), and Hank Johnson (Ga.). The amendment was sponsored by Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-FL), who had warned colleagues she would 'BLOW UP the farm bill' over the issue. Luna said during debate that her own party had pushed back hard against her (including a Republican who, the night before, had called her a 'damn liar') and added on the floor: 'I never thought I'd have to be debating liability protections for pesticide companies. Yet here I am today.' House Agriculture Chair G.T. Thompson (R-PA) led the opposing effort and defended the original language to Politico: 'It would prevent frivolous lawsuits if it's in compliance with the science that the EPA has put forward. I think this is a tool that's really important for food affordability, because these are tools are important for yield, to be able to feed the nation, feed the world.' Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-ME), who has resisted similar provisions in past appropriations and farm bills, joined Luna and told the chamber: 'This amendment is not extreme. It would not ban pesticides or require any additional regulatory burden on the manufacturers. Quite literally it would preserve the status quo and allow the Supreme Court to examine this issue separately and the complicated legal issues at its core.' The stripped provisions would have shielded pesticide manufacturers (including Bayer, the maker of Roundup) from state-law failure-to-warn lawsuits, the same legal mechanism at issue in Monsanto v. Durnell, the case the Supreme Court heard three days earlier. This marks the second time in 2026 that this Bayer-backed liability language has been killed by a MAHA-Democrat coalition; the first came in January, when it was stripped from the 2026 EPA appropriations bill before House Republicans revived it in the farm-bill markup in March.
title: House Strikes Pesticide Liability Shield 280–142 in MAHA-Led Vote — Essential Democratic Support Made the Win Possible

description: Cross-partisan pressure from MAHA activists and Democratic lawmakers succeeded in stripping the pesticide liability shield from the House farm bill. The provision (backed by Bayer and the broader chemical industry) would have prevented states and courts from holding pesticide manufacturers accountable for failing to warn consumers about health risks beyond what the EPA recognizes, effectively shielding Roundup and similar products from failure-to-warn litigation. In an interview with The Hill / NewsNation, Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-ME) explains why she joined the bipartisan effort. The win marks the second time MAHA-aligned advocates and Democratic legislators have together killed this same Bayer-backed language: it was first stripped from the 2026 EPA appropriations bill in January after a 'hard fight' (per Pingree), then revived by House Republicans in the farm bill markup in March. The pressure campaign documented elsewhere on this timeline, the April 8 Pingree-Ryerson joint op-ed in The Hill, the April 27 'People v. Poison' rally outside the Supreme Court during oral arguments in Monsanto v. Durnell, culminated in this April 30 outcome. It is also one of the clearest demonstrations to date of the cross-partisan health coalition this site argues is necessary: a movement organized around enforceable chemical accountability rather than partisan loyalty.
title: Watch: Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-ME) on Killing the Farm Bill's Pesticide Liability Shield

description: The video above is from an April 28 hearing of the House Energy and Commerce Environment Subcommittee, where Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) confronted EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin with FOIA'd visitor logs and internal EPA emails after he denied meeting with Bayer about its ongoing Roundup litigation. As Ocasio-Cortez's office and her own X post document, Zeldin first told the committee, 'No, I never did,' then revised that to say the meeting had been 'very brief.' Ocasio-Cortez then produced documents obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request showing Bayer's CEO, vice president, and lobbyist had met with Zeldin's EPA before the company's executive-order push and its Supreme Court filing in Monsanto v. Durnell, with the visitor logs and emails listing the meeting topic as 'legal/judicial issues.' One internal email Ocasio-Cortez quoted on the record: 'In this internal email, it says that Bayer was specifically seeking and discussing Supreme Court action, it would want an update on EPA's regulatory review, and that, interestingly, Bayer will provide a small thanks for updating the glyphosate webpage from the EPA and work on MAHA.' Reporting by Investigate Midwest places the 'small thanks' language in fuller context: Bayer's outreach signaled that EPA's withdrawal of support for California's cancer-warning label and its edits to the glyphosate webpage directly reinforced the company's federal-preemption argument before the Supreme Court, the case Monsanto v. Durnell hinged on EPA not warning the American public about Roundup. The New Republic framed the hearing as part of a broader pattern in which Zeldin has tried to avoid MAHA critics even as the agency he leads has aligned its actions with the very chemical manufacturers MAHA campaigns against.
