When pressed by Ocasio-Cortez on the apparent conflict of interest, Zeldin did not directly answer and pointed instead to the EPA's pending review of glyphosate, due later this year. The exchange exposes the gap between the Trump administration's stated MAHA priorities and the EPA's behind-the-scenes coordination with the company at the center of the Supreme Court case heard the day before.
title: Watch: AOC Confronts EPA's Zeldin With FOIA'd Visitor Logs Showing Hidden Bayer Meetings

description: On April 27, the Supreme Court heard oral arguments in Monsanto v. Durnell, a case brought by a Missouri man who says he developed cancer after using Roundup. The Court will decide whether plaintiffs harmed by pesticide exposure can continue to bring state-law failure-to-warn claims against chemical manufacturers, a question with sweeping implications for MAHA's anti-pesticide agenda. Outside the Court, several hundred people assembled for the 'People v. Poison' rally, an unusual cross-partisan coalition of MAHA activists, environmentalists, Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY), Sen. Cory Booker (D-NJ), and former Democratic congressman Dennis Kucinich. Kucinich told the crowd the case will decide 'whether or not states have a fundamental right to be able to stand up for the health and safety of their people and give people access to due process at a state level' and warned that if the Court sides with Bayer, the justices 'will have taken down a cornerstone of our country.' Sarah Starman, a third-generation farmer with Friends of the Earth, framed the moment as a paradox: 'The Trump administration has gutted protections for health and for the environment. But at the same time, the public momentum against pesticides and behind cleaning up toxic chemicals in our environment and behind healthy food and farming is so strong.' The full livestream of the rally is archived at thepeoplevspoison.org/live. Inside the courtroom, the justices appeared divided. The legal question, laid out in detail by SCOTUSblog, is not whether glyphosate is carcinogenic, but whether a 1972 federal pesticide statute supersedes states' authority to require their own product labels. Justice Brett Kavanaugh emphasized concerns about a fragmented patchwork of state labels; Chief Justice John Roberts pressed the opposite point, questioning what role states might retain during EPA's lengthy review timeline: 'If it turns out that they were right, it might have been good if they had an opportunity to do something to call this danger to the attention of the people while the federal government was going through its process.' US Solicitor General D. John Sauer filed a brief on behalf of the Trump administration backing Bayer, writing that 'EPA has repeatedly determined that glyphosate is not likely to be carcinogenic in humans, and the agency has repeatedly approved RoundUp labels that did not contain cancer warnings.' A Bayer spokesperson said a ruling in the company's favor would 'provide essential regulatory clarity for companies.' Bayer has already paid out billions in Roundup-related claims and proposed an additional settlement of up to $7.25 billion in February. The case carries particular irony for Kennedy, whose breakthrough as an environmental lawyer came in 2018 when he helped win a $289 million jury award (later reduced to $20.4 million) for DeWayne 'Lee' Johnson, a San Francisco school groundskeeper diagnosed with terminal non-Hodgkin's lymphoma at 42 after years of Roundup exposure. At a budget hearing the day after the rally, lawmakers pressed Kennedy on his earlier promises to rein in glyphosate. He said he was 'very clear with the president about my own displeasure with the executive order' boosting domestic glyphosate production but defended Trump's reasoning: 'The president felt it was necessary for national security reasons.' Asked directly whether glyphosate causes cancer, Kennedy answered: 'Yes.' MAHA podcaster Alex Clark, who attended the April 9 Oval Office meeting (covered separately on this timeline), facilitated according to CNN by Erika Kirk and MAHA allies inside the administration, told CNN: 'Mothers do not want their kids poisoned by pesticides that cannot wash off produce and they cannot get away from, and they're breathing it in, in the air. That is what matters to moms. And nobody votes, and nobody rallies, and nobody shows up to the polls, or doesn't show up to the polls if they're mad, like a mother. This is the No. 1 group that you do not want to piss off and that you do not want to lose on your side.' Vani Hari ('Food Babe') predicted: 'Glyphosate is going to be a midterm issue because the Trump administration made it an issue.' A SCOTUS decision is expected in June. The EPA's court-ordered glyphosate safety review is due in October (weeks before the midterms) though a provision tucked into the House farm bill would delay it to 2031.
title: SCOTUS Hears Monsanto v. Durnell as MAHA Rallies Outside in 'People v. Poison' Demonstration

description: A New York Times investigation by Lisa Friedman documents that in one year, the EPA's Office of Research and Development, a 50-year-old scientific arm that produced foundational work on fertility, asthma, wildfires, drinking water, and climate change, has been almost entirely dismantled. More than 1,500 biologists, chemists, toxicologists, and other experts have been laid off, reassigned, or pressured to retire. Only 124 researchers remain, and this month they must decide whether to abandon their work or relocate to different parts of the agency or the country. Those who stay will lose the firewall that historically separated scientists from political appointees: an internal memo reviewed by the Times notes that future research must 'align with agency and administration priorities.' The cuts have closed the only laboratory of its kind in the world for controlled human-exposure tests on vehicle exhaust, wildfire smoke, and ozone; reassigned the team that detected the forever-chemical GenX in North Carolina's Cape Fear River Basin; and eliminated EPA's dedicated climate-science researchers entirely. Jennifer Orme-Zavaleta, who led the research office during the first Trump administration, told the Times the agency 'just blew up a very well-performing organization that was making a difference, not only in the country but in the world,' adding that 'there's really nobody anymore that will be looking out, with a comprehensive, independent perspective, at the quality of our environment and the quality of our health.' The dismantling executes a Project 2025 priority: the conservative blueprint's EPA chapter, written by Mandy Gunasekara, who served as agency chief of staff during the first Trump term, described the science office as 'bloated, unaccountable, closed, outcome-driven, hostile to public and legislative input, and inclined to pursue political rather than purely scientific goals.' Eighty industry trade groups had previously attacked the office's chemical-risk evaluations as 'out of step with global health agencies and regulators.' Also gutted: epidemiology, the discipline behind the landmark Harvard Six Cities study that linked air pollution to shorter life expectancy and triggered stricter EPA air-quality standards. Six Cities principal investigator Douglas Dockery said industry attempts to weaken epidemiology had failed for decades, but this time, 'They're just saying, "We're getting rid of all the science."' Former scientists describe the human cost. Bryan Hubbell, who led the air, climate, and energy program, took early retirement after 27 years: 'I knew I wasn't going to be able to keep doing the work.' Environmental epidemiologist Thomas J. Luben said his work disappeared overnight: 'The first week of the Trump administration, there was no more environmental justice, and no more climate change.' Luben was later fired for signing a letter accusing the administration of 'recklessly undermining the E.P.A. mission' and is appealing on First Amendment grounds. Joel Hoffman, a 19-year EPA biologist at the Great Lakes Toxicology and Ecology Division in Duluth, resigned, telling the Times: 'If you simply withhold funding and stall programs, you can functionally end the research without ever saying, "We've ended the research."' Earl Gray, a 40-year toxicologist who evaluated reproductive damage from chemical exposure, summarized the deregulatory logic: 'If you have no data I guess you can just assume things are safe.' Zeldin's spokeswoman Brigit Hirsch dismissed the concerns as 'an absurd narrative from people who know better and union rumor mills' and said 'Gold-standard science is happening like never before at the Trump E.P.A.' Gunasekara called the changes 'merely structural,' arguing that 'characterizing this as getting rid of science is very misleading.' The agency has also stopped quantifying the value of a human life when setting emissions limits and, under Zeldin, has repealed or weakened more than two dozen regulations covering power plants, vehicle tailpipes, and oil and gas wells. The implications for MAHA's anti-chemical agenda are direct: without independent EPA scientists generating data on PFAS, pesticides, or other exposures, the evidentiary basis for restricting toxic chemicals, including the very glyphosate and PFAS exposures MAHA campaigns against, may simply cease to be produced.
title: NYT: EPA's Independent Science Office Almost Entirely Dismantled in One Year

description: A New Yorker investigation, headlined 'Can the EPA Survive Lee Zeldin?' and posted April 27 ahead of the magazine's May 4 issue, walks readers through a year of structural damage at the EPA. President Trump has called Zeldin 'one of the superstars' of his second administration and 'our secret weapon,' and the piece argues that the praise is earned: by the New Yorker's reporting, the agency now operates as a near-open ally of the industries it was created to regulate. Five threads stand out. (1) Scope of the demolition. Industry lobbyists now fill key senior posts. Public-facing data archives have been pulled offline. Whole offices have been closed. Long-standing limits on arsenic, mercury, and PM2.5 fine soot have all been thrown out, and the agency has formally embraced coal. EPA staffing is down roughly 25% under Zeldin, with more than 700 of those departures holding doctorates. (2) The endangerment finding. Zeldin's most consequential legal move is his repeal of the 2009 endangerment finding, the determination, signed under Obama, that greenhouse gases threaten public welfare, and the foundation of every federal climate rule since. Even Trump's first-term EPA chief Scott Pruitt left it alone. Zeldin became the first administrator to attack the underlying premise of EPA's authority over carbon dioxide. Twenty-four states have sued, and the case is widely expected to land at the Supreme Court, where Zeldin is reportedly betting the three Trump-appointed Justices will help reverse the 2007 ruling that compelled the finding. Former Obama-era EPA chief Gina McCarthy told the New Yorker the legal rationale is 'absolutely ludicrous, but that doesn't mean that it won't go all the way to the Supreme Court, and it doesn't mean that this Supreme Court might not uphold it.' If the Court does reverse, future EPAs would have no statutory basis to regulate carbon dioxide absent action by Congress. (3) Retaliation for the staff letter. A letter from over 150 EPA employees last summer urged Zeldin to 'correct course,' citing his 'politicized messaging,' his hollowing-out of the agency's research division, and his habit of brushing aside scientists' conclusions. Emails later disclosed by E&E News showed that EPA's own lawyers had told leadership the letter raised no ethical concerns and that 'government employee speech is protected.' Zeldin proceeded anyway, suspending 144 of the signatories on administrative leave and announcing: 'We have a ZERO tolerance policy for agency bureaucrats unlawfully undermining, sabotaging, and undercutting the agenda of this administration.' (4) MAHA-washing. After MAHA leader Kelly Ryerson launched a petition demanding Zeldin's removal, flagging two former American Chemistry Council lobbyists Zeldin had placed in the EPA's chemical-safety division and his sign-off on new PFAS-adjacent pesticides, Zeldin pivoted to engagement. He hosted MAHA moms at agency headquarters in late December and then announced a string of so-called 'MAHA wins,' including a phthalate rule and a paraquat reassessment. The New Yorker reports that both were largely cosmetic: the phthalate rule covers only worker exposure, not the consumer-product exposure to children that MAHA actually campaigns about, and the paraquat reassessment was an inheritance from a Biden-era decision four years prior. Nathan Donley of the Center for Biological Diversity gave the pattern a name: 'Much like the greenwashing you see at the grocery store, with terms like eco-friendly or green advertising chemical-laden products on store shelves, Zeldin's MAHA-washing paints the same rosy picture to distract from decisions that harm public health.' MAHA podcaster Alex Clark told the New Yorker that despite Zeldin's outreach, 'In the EPA, you see this massive gap where the revolving door seems to still be shuffling people in.' (5) Generational damage. Many of Zeldin's actions face ongoing litigation, and a future administrator could in theory reinstate some of the rules he killed. But former EPA administrator William Reilly told the New Yorker the deeper losses are not recoverable: 'It was a little like Zuckerberg: move fast and break things. It will take a while for the courts to catch up. And, by the time they do, the scientists, the lawyers, the engineers, they will have gone somewhere else. They will no longer be recoverable.' An Environmental Defense Fund analysis cited in the piece estimates that EPA's rollbacks (paired with the elimination of clean-energy tax credits) will add roughly 1.5 billion tons of CO2 to the atmosphere through 2030 and approximately 12 billion tons through 2040, with warming and sea-level effects that persist for centuries. The article concludes that the projected premature-death count from the deregulatory campaign 'could easily run to the tens of thousands.' The piece complements the same-day NYT investigation by Lisa Friedman (covered in a separate April 27 entry) on the dismantling of EPA's Office of Research and Development, and provides additional context for AOC's April 28 confrontation of Zeldin with FOIA'd Bayer documents (also on this timeline).
title: New Yorker: 'Can the EPA Survive Lee Zeldin?' — A Comprehensive Map of the Agency's Year-One Demolition

description: At the 'People v. Poison' rally outside the U.S. Supreme Court on April 27, MAHA leader Vani Hari ('The Food Babe') (a co-organizer of the demonstration) opens the day by setting the stakes for the assembled crowd. Bayer, she tells protesters, is asking the Court to give it what amounts to a total pass on glyphosate: blanket immunity from future failure-to-warn lawsuits brought by Americans who developed cancer after years of exposure to Roundup. The protest was timed deliberately to coincide with the first day of oral arguments in Monsanto v. Durnell, the case in which Bayer is seeking that immunity, and which the Trump Justice Department is backing on the company's side through Solicitor General D. John Sauer's brief urging the Court to find that EPA's labeling regime preempts state failure-to-warn claims. The clip captures the cross-partisan tone of the event Hari helped build: a coalition of MAHA activists, environmentalists, Democrats, and Republicans converging on the Court steps in defense of ordinary Americans' right to sue when chemical companies fail to warn them about the health risks of their products. The full livestream of the rally is archived at thepeoplevspoison.org/live. (For the full news coverage of the SCOTUS oral arguments and the rally, see the companion April 27 entry on this timeline.)
title: Watch: Vani Hari ('Food Babe') Opens 'People v. Poison' Rally as Bayer Seeks SCOTUS Immunity

description: A New York Times report by Sheryl Gay Stolberg finds the MAHA movement growing disillusioned with Trump and Republicans seven months before the November midterms. Six of the movement's most visible leaders (together commanding millions of social media followers) told the Times in separate interviews that the predominantly female voters who followed Kennedy into Trump's camp are demoralized enough to potentially stay home in November. Turning Point USA podcaster Alex Clark warned: 'Republicans would be stupid, moronic, to let these voters just slip through our fingers.' She added that MAHA voters 'have nowhere to go. They feel like their vote is useless. They have lost the energy. They have lost the enthusiasm. They feel like the Democrats don't care about them. They feel like the Republicans lied to them, and they're not planning on voting.' The piece documents three major fractures inside the coalition: vaccine skeptics complain the White House is silencing Kennedy on the issue that originally defined him; Dr. Casey Means, Trump's surgeon general nominee and a MAHA favorite, remains stalled in the Senate; and food and anti-pesticide advocates feel deceived by Trump's glyphosate executive order. Vani Hari ('The Food Babe') said: 'It's very hard to support a movement that is labeled MAHA when two opposing things are happening at the same time. It's like, "Yes, we can eat all the real food we want, but it's covered in Roundup."' Zen Honeycutt of Moms Across America underscored the movement's independence from either party: 'The only thing that matters is action. Not a political party.' Leslie Manookian of the Health Freedom Defense Fund described MAHA as 'a populist, grass roots movement' with no single leader. The MAHA PAC, run by Kennedy ally Tony Lyons, set a $100 million target in March to elect MAHA-aligned Republicans but had raised only $1.2 million through the end of February. Democrats are beginning to see the opening. Sen. Cory Booker filed an amicus brief supporting the plaintiff in Monsanto v. Durnell, the glyphosate failure-to-warn case the Supreme Court will hear April 27. Democratic pollster Celinda Lake distinguishes between vaccine-focused MAHA voters (who are unlikely to back Democrats) and food- and organic-focused voters, whom Kennedy calls 'MAHA Moms' and Lake calls 'Organic Moms.' She argues Democrats lost that latter group in 2024 by ignoring their priorities: 'There is an incredible opening for Democrats, and we should not miss this opportunity.' Rep. Chellie Pingree will speak at the April 27 'People v. Poison' rally outside the Supreme Court. She told the Times she increasingly tells Democratic colleagues they are blowing a major opportunity on food and pesticides: 'The reason Donald Trump ran on them, the reason he put R.F.K. in office, is because people care about them. We should be all over this.' The article notes Sen. Bill Cassidy, chair of the Senate health committee, has yet to schedule a confirmation vote for Dr. Means; the MAHA PAC is backing his primary challenger, setting up an early electoral test when Louisiana holds its primary next month. In 2015, the International Agency for Research on Cancer deemed glyphosate 'probably carcinogenic to humans'; the EPA has disagreed and does not require a warning label.
title: NYT: MAHA Coalition Strains; Democrats See Midterm Opening with 'Organic Moms'

description: The Trump administration's push to restrict what SNAP recipients can buy is producing an uneven, state-by-state rollout that is frustrating low-income shoppers, confusing independent grocers, and generating legal challenges, according to a Washington Post investigation. As of mid-April, 22 mostly Republican-led states have received federal USDA waivers to reshape the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, a scope of restriction the agency had previously rejected, including Mike Bloomberg's 2011 New York City sugary-drink proposal and Maine's request during the first Trump term. Ten states have now implemented their changes. All 22 approved states limit some drinks; 14 also limit candy. But because USDA declined to issue uniform federal definitions, the same product can qualify in one state and be ineligible a few miles away. Candy containing flour (KitKats, Twix) often remains eligible, while sparkling water, electrolyte drinks such as Pedialyte, and certain cold sandwiches may not. States have taken divergent approaches to guiding retailers: some published long lists of ineligible product codes, while others declined. Third-party firms have stepped in to sell compliance lists, which a West Virginia spokeswoman said cost $130,000 for a one-time version the state deemed 'cost prohibitive.' Independent grocers warn the inconsistent enforcement could jeopardize their SNAP participation. OFW Law principal Stewart Fried, who represents retailers, said USDA's failure to set national definitions 'has created massive confusion across the entire country.' HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has framed the effort as ending taxpayer dollars for products tied to chronic disease. At a February Austin rally he said: 'If somebody wants to buy a Coke in this country, they ought to be able to do it. The taxpayer shouldn't have to fund it for children. ... We're giving them diabetes and then we're paying for it. The whole system is insane.' Anti-hunger advocates and some SNAP recipients disagree. Iowa participant Marc Craig, a plaintiff in a multi-state lawsuit against the new rules, asked: 'How does limiting me getting a healthy sandwich and letting me eat cookies and cake make me healthier?' Retired NYU nutrition scholar Marion Nestle described herself as conflicted, arguing against taxpayer-subsidized sugary drinks while warning the rules risk stigmatizing low-income Americans. HHS spokesman Andrew Nixon said the agency is 'clear that we will support efforts by states to pursue SNAP waivers that prioritize healthier food options.' The pilot period runs two years, and USDA says it is 'working with retailers, not penalizing minor, inadvertent mistakes,' though enforcement has begun in at least five states after a 90-day grace period.
title: SNAP Candy and Soda Bans Roll Out Across 22 States — With Confusion and Lawsuits

description: In a New York Times opinion essay, Dr. Rachael Bedard, a geriatrician and palliative care physician who contributes to the Times opinion section, argues that MAHA's electoral muscle has been overstated and the movement is better understood as a determined special-interest constituency than a swing-voter bloc capable of deciding elections. Bedard opens with a scene from Kennedy's late-February 'Eat Real Food' rally in Austin, where a Steak 'n' Shake food truck handed out free burgers and fries in beef tallow, a band billed as 'swampadelic country rock' warmed up the crowd, and supporters waved posters of steak and whole milk, before turning to the political math. She cites the POLITICO/Public First poll already on this timeline: while 48% said they supported MAHA, only 34% could explain what it is, and only 31% identified as part of the movement. More damaging, voters ranked 'Americans are too unhealthy' near the bottom of their issue priorities, in a tie with 'wokeism' and below climate change and gun rights, well behind cost of living and the economy. Bedard's conclusion: Kennedy has limited leverage with GOP leaders because Republican strategists know most voters will not cast their ballot on MAHA's agenda. A February memo from MAHA Action to GOP committees made the opposite case, calling the movement 'a once in a generation political gift to the G.O.P.' and warning, in what Bedard characterizes as mob-boss style, that 'Republicans who failed to embrace the gift of the MAGA movement have had their political careers meet an untimely demise. Republicans serving now shouldn't make the same mistake and fail to embrace the gift of MAHA.' Steve Bannon's 2025 prediction to former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene appears too: 'If you merge MAHA and MAGA, it's like 1932: You govern forever.' But Bedard argues the White House has begun unwinding the merger from its end. On vaccines (the issue most associated with Kennedy) two Republican pollsters argued last year that 'Vaccine skepticism is bad politics,' and the administration appears to agree: a federal judge enjoined Kennedy's vaccine advisory committee changes, surgeon general nominee Dr. Casey Means now looks doomed in the Senate after she gave equivocal answers about vaccines at her confirmation hearing, and an unnamed White House official told Bedard, 'We're just kind of done with the vaccine issue.' Charles Eisenstein, who wrote speeches for Kennedy's 2024 presidential campaign, told the Times that during that campaign, 'We did our very best to get him to avoid the issue like the plague.' Kennedy himself has stopped mentioning vaccines in recent appearances, Bedard reports, even as MAHA-aligned groups (Children's Health Defense, the MAHA Institute, the Brownstone Institute) continue to litigate, lobby, and back state-level mandate rollbacks now under consideration in Oklahoma, Hawaii, New York, and West Virginia. On glyphosate, Bedard suggests Trump's February executive order may be Kennedy's 'Sister Souljah moment', a calculated public break with his base meant to win over GOP establishment skeptics. The MAHA reaction was instant: anti-glyphosate activist Kelly Ryerson called the executive order 'America Last, Anti-MAHA and unforgivable,' and Alex Clark posted that 'Moms across the country reveal they are unlikely to vote red in the midterms BECAUSE OF THE GLYPHOSATE EXECUTIVE ORDER.' Ryerson, who attended the April 9 White House meeting (covered separately on this timeline), told Bedard the meeting was 'promising' but said 'very real actions' must follow before November if Republicans 'hope to keep MAHA showing up at the voting booth.' Bedard closes with a forecast: rumors are circulating that Kennedy may exit HHS, and she notes he has begun quietly testing new political material, a recent Nashville speech focused on prescription drug price negotiations and rural hospital subsidies, that could anchor a future presidential run built on populist, anti-corporate health-care reform. Her parting line: Kennedy 'isn't a zealot for a cause; he's just another man who wants to run the world, hiding in plain sight. MAHA moms, however, are potentially too committed to sacrifice their goals even in service of their leader's ambition.'
title: NYT Opinion: Bedard Argues MAHA's Electoral Clout Has Been Overstated

description: On April 9, with MAHA activists increasingly angry at the Trump administration, the White House convened a private meeting with three prominent movement influencers, a bid to shore up a coalition the GOP had hoped would deliver women and independent voters in November. Among the attendees was activist Courtney Swan, who declared herself disillusioned last month: 'It's starting to feel like both sides are in on it, and we're being scammed.' The outreach came at a low point for HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., whose authority inside the administration has visibly narrowed since Trump's executive order boosting domestic production of the weedkiller glyphosate, a move that triggered some of the most intense backlash MAHA has mounted against the White House to date. In a West Wing round-table running more than an hour, the influencers pressed senior officials on glyphosate and the sluggish pace of food-policy reform. Listening on the administration's side were Kennedy, Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, and other senior aides, who responded by highlighting achievements such as the redesigned federal food pyramid. Trump then brought the group into the Oval Office for more than 20 minutes, praising Kennedy's performance and (after a joke about Diet Coke clashing with a healthy image) pressing the red button on the Resolute Desk, which summoned a staffer bearing a glass bottle. The attendees departed with Trump challenge coins in gold and their choice of MAGA merchandise; Turning Point USA podcaster Alex Clark took a 'Trump 2028' hat, she said, 'to troll the libs.' Also at the table was Dr. Casey Means, Trump's stalled surgeon general nominee. Clark told officials Means was 'trustworthy to the MAHA base' and argued her confirmation would help the administration reach the movement. Clark described leaving the meeting feeling 'hopeful, and grateful for an opportunity to have a face-to-face conversation and be heard by all of President Trump's top advisers.' Swan, who walked in skeptical, said afterward: 'They were asking questions with curiosity. To me as someone who was fighting his fight for so long, I was blown away.' White House spokesman Kush Desai said the administration 'regularly meets with the MAHA community to hear their concerns and advice.' The charm offensive came less than two weeks after a POLITICO poll found 41% of Trump's own 2024 voters believe his administration has not done enough on MAHA priorities. Additional coverage: WSJ · Politico Pulse · Politico Pro.
title: Trump Brings MAHA Influencers Into the Oval Office as Discontent Grows

description: Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-ME), a longtime organic farmer serving on the House Agriculture Committee, and Kelly Ryerson (the MAHA movement leader known online as 'Glyphosate Girl') jointly published an op-ed in The Hill announcing a cross-ideological alliance ahead of two major pesticide-policy battles. They argue that Americans across the political spectrum agree on three points: food should be free of harmful chemicals; people should receive clear warnings about potential health risks; and chemical manufacturers should not get legal protection when their products sicken consumers. The op-ed highlights two imminent flashpoints. First, the House is preparing to vote on a farm bill containing what the authors call provisions drafted by the chemical industry that would broaden federal preemption of state pesticide rules, remove the authority of states and communities to mandate consumer warnings about health risks, and create a liability shield for chemical manufacturers. Pingree offered a committee amendment to strike the language; nearly every Democrat supported it, and no Republican did. Seven states, including Maine, have their own local pesticide laws and health-warning rules that the new language would preempt. Second, on April 27, the Supreme Court will hear Monsanto v. Durnell, a case testing whether people harmed by pesticide exposure can continue to bring state-law failure-to-warn claims. Pingree and Ryerson plan to join a 'People vs. Poison' rally outside the Court that morning with advocates and MAHA supporters from across the political spectrum. The authors note Bayer has paid roughly $10 billion in Roundup-related settlements and has proposed setting aside up to $7.25 billion more for current and future claims. They highlight that EPA pesticide risk reviews occur only every 15 years, and glyphosate's most recent full review dates to 1993. They also argue that the White House's backing of Bayer (including Trump's executive order boosting domestic glyphosate production) drew fury from Kennedy's MAHA base, whose supporters interpreted it as a betrayal, and exposed what they call 'a live fault line in American politics.' 'You do not have to agree on everything to agree on this,' the authors conclude: 'Our families deserve honest warnings, our communities deserve the right to protect themselves, and Big Chemical should not be above the law.'
title: Pingree and 'Glyphosate Girl' Co-Author Op-Ed Against Farm Bill Pesticide Shield

description: On April 30, the House voted 280–142 to remove Section 10205 from the 2026 farm bill: language that would have reaffirmed the EPA as the sole authority on pesticide labeling, effectively shielding Bayer/Monsanto and other manufacturers from state-law failure-to-warn lawsuits like the one heard at the Supreme Court three days earlier in Monsanto v. Durnell. The Luna Amendment, sponsored by Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-FL), passed only because of overwhelming Democratic support. Among Democrats: 207 yes, 6 no, near-unanimous. Among Republicans: 73 yes (the MAHA-aligned wing) and 136 no, meaning the MAHA faction was outvoted nearly two-to-one inside its own caucus. Without the Democratic bloc, the MAHA-led effort would have failed. The broader farm bill passed the House 224–200 the same morning; the amendment must still survive Senate negotiations and reconciliation before becoming law.
title: House Strips Pesticide Liability Shield from Farm Bill (Luna Amendment, 280–142)

description: The 2026 farm bill, which passed the House 224–200 on April 30, declined to reverse the roughly $187 billion in SNAP cuts enacted through the prior year's tax-and-spending reconciliation package (the "One Big Beautiful Bill"). SNAP is the federal nutrition program through which more than 40 million low-income Americans purchase food; cuts of this scale directly undermine MAHA's stated mission of expanding access to healthier food, especially for children. Anti-hunger groups criticized the farm bill for failing to undo the cuts. The bill's separate Luna Amendment win on pesticide liability does not offset its silence on food access for the lowest-income Americans, and the new SNAP candy/soda restrictions rolling out across 22 states (covered separately on this site's timeline) further narrow what shrunken SNAP benefits can buy.
title: 2026 Farm Bill Leaves $187B in SNAP Cuts Intact

description: A POLITICO/Public First poll (Mar. 13–18, n=3,851) finds that most Americans believe the Trump administration has not done enough to 'Make America Healthy Again', including a 41% plurality of Trump's own 2024 voters. While 47% of Americans support the MAHA movement overall (including roughly a third of Harris 2024 voters), Democrats are seen as more trustworthy on health priorities and less influenced by food and pesticide industry lobbyists than Republicans. MAHA supporters' top priorities, stricter PFAS regulation, halting infectious diseases, expanding reproductive health access, align more closely with Democratic positions than Republican ones. MAHA Action president Tony Lyons has warned the GOP it is only "renting MAHA voters" and hasn't been able to "purchase" them, and that dissatisfied MAHA voters peeling off or staying home in November could cost Republicans control of Congress. GOP strategist Abby McCloskey said the initial MAHA energy has 'trickled off.' Despite the vulnerabilities, health ranks low as a top voter priority, and some MAHA-aligned policies (removing artificial dyes, offering whole milk in schools) retain broad support.
title: POLITICO Poll: Most Americans — Including 41% of Trump Voters — Say Admin Has Not Done Enough on MAHA

description: A first-of-its-kind Environmental Working Group analysis of California Department of Pesticide Regulation testing records found PFAS pesticide residues on 37% of conventional California produce. About 90% of peaches, plums, and nectarines tested positive for PFAS, as did 80% of strawberries and grapes. EWG's Bernadette Del Chiaro flagged particular concern for children, who commonly eat these fruits and face greater risk from PFAS's toxic effects. The analysis coincided with the introduction of California legislation that would ban PFAS as active ingredients in pesticides by 2035 and require warning labels in the interim. The findings add pressure to the EPA, which has continued approving new PFAS-based pesticides under the Trump administration despite MAHA's stated mission to reduce children's chemical exposures.
title: EWG Analysis: PFAS Residues Found on 37% of Conventional California Produce

description: Kennedy told a podcast ('The Bossticks') that aired Monday that the GRAS loophole had already been closed: 'We've changed the GRAS loophole so that we've closed it. So the new ingredients have to show safety studies.' HHS spokesman Richard Danker quickly walked it back, clarifying Kennedy 'was referring to our proposed GRAS rule making and its potential application if finalized.' The rule is still awaiting White House clearance before it can even be published as a proposed rule. Food industry trade groups, bakers, tree nut processors, chemical distributors, and dietary supplement makers, have preemptively lobbied the White House against the measure, warning it would exceed FDA's statutory authority and trigger litigation. 'If F.D.A. would come in and say, You have to file it with us, it's not what the law says,' said food industry lawyer Todd Harrison. 'I think F.D.A. loses that case.' State-level bans in West Virginia and Texas are already facing industry lawsuits. EWG's Melanie Benesh noted: 'At the federal level, we just have not yet seen that kind of lasting, enforceable regulatory action.'
title: RFK Jr. Falsely Claims GRAS Loophole Closed — Industry Vows to Sue

description: More Perfect Union interviews MAHA supporters who voted for Trump specifically on the promise of cleaning up the food supply and reining in the chemical industry, and are now grappling with evidence that the administration has stocked the EPA's pesticide office with former industry lobbyists. Zen Honeycutt, a prominent MAHA activist, articulates the tension directly: she still wants to believe the administration will change course, but the facts on the ground are hard to ignore. Four former chemical industry representatives (including ex-American Chemistry Council officials and American Soybean Association lobbyist Kyle Kunkler) now hold senior roles at the EPA's Office of Chemical Safety. Internal calendars show a 25-to-1 ratio of corporate to public health meetings. Nathan Donley of the Center for Biological Diversity is more direct, saying MAHA supporters are being offered scraps while the chemical industry receives sweeping regulatory relief behind closed doors.
title: More Perfect Union: MAHA Supporters Confront the Administration's Ties to Big Ag and the Chemical Industry

description: A report from the Iowa Environmental Council and the Harkin Institute links Iowa's cancer burden to four environmental exposures — pesticides, nitrates, PFAS and radon — and singles out the three agricultural chemicals used most heavily in the state: glyphosate, acetochlor and atrazine. The underlying numbers are stark. Iowa has the second-highest cancer rate in the country and is one of only three states, with Utah and West Virginia, where incidence is still climbing. The rate tracked the national average until 2012, then began rising for reasons nobody has pinned down, reaching roughly 506 cases per 100,000 people in 2022 against a national figure of 442. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma and acute myeloid leukemia are both elevated. A separate Food & Water Watch analysis found raised rates of lymphatic cancer in 82% of the counties that spray the most. The picture is not uncontested: the Iowa Cancer Registry has reported that agricultural communities in the state show lower rates than the statewide average for most cancers, and Sarah Green of the Iowa Environmental Council says the causes remain unclear. The findings land in an election year in which cancer would outrank the cost of living in at least one survey of Iowa voters.
title: Iowa Report Ties the State's Rising Cancer Rate to Pesticides, Nitrates, PFAS and Radon

description: Saturday Night Live, hosted by Harry Styles, airs a sketch titled 'MAHAspital,' a parody of the medical drama The Pitt reimagined as a hospital run by RFK Jr., played by cast member James Austin Johnson. The sketch marks the MAHA movement's arrival as a subject of mainstream late-night satire.
title: SNL 'MAHAspital' Sketch Parodies RFK Jr. and the MAHA Movement

description: The Trump Interior Department proposed replacing a Biden-era rule that required oil and gas companies to post $6.9 billion in bonds to cover offshore platform cleanup costs in the event of bankruptcy. The new rule would save the industry $484 million per year in compliance costs. A 2024 GAO report had found taxpayers exposed to billions in risk if offshore operators fail to meet decommissioning obligations; the rollback shifts that liability back to the public.
title: Trump Proposes Rolling Back Offshore Oil Decommissioning Bonds

description: Kennedy keynotes the MAHA Rally for Real Food in Austin. He frames federal procurement ($405M/day for school lunches, WIC, SNAP, and Head Start) as the primary lever to reshape the food system. He touts the GRAS loophole closure, the new food pyramid, and the food dye phase-out as major wins.
title: MAHA Rally for Real Food — Austin, Texas

description: HHS and the Dept. of Education convened leaders from 53 top medical schools across 31 states to commit to requiring at least 40 hours of nutrition education for students beginning fall 2026. Secretaries Kennedy and McMahon were joined by the presidents of the AMA, AAMC, and AACOM. The commitment is a meaningful shift in how the medical profession approaches diet and chronic disease. That said, its impact is limited in scope: it affects future physicians only, carries no enforcement mechanism, and does not address the structural conditions (food deserts, ultra-processed food dominance, agricultural subsidies) that shape what most Americans actually eat. Without accompanying regulatory and financial reforms, better-trained doctors will have limited tools to act on what they know.
title: 53 Medical Schools Commit to Mandatory Nutrition Training

description: House Republicans include nearly identical pesticide-protection language in the new farm bill, preventing states and courts from penalizing pesticide makers for health warnings beyond EPA recognition. MAHA allies are outraged that the provision stripped from the appropriations bill has resurfaced. The Environmental Working Group calls it a 'betrayal of MAHA.' Republican leadership stands by the measure despite pressure from the movement.
title: House GOP Farm Bill Revives Pesticide Liability Shield

description: A Senate Republican proposal included in budget reconciliation would gut key provisions of TSCA, the primary federal law governing chemical safety, stripping EPA's ability to evaluate and restrict dangerous chemicals in consumer products, food, and the environment. The proposal would weaken new-chemical review requirements and limit EPA oversight authority.
title: Senate Republicans Propose Weakening Toxic Substances Control Act

description: Kennedy posts an AI-generated retro action figure commercial to his official HHS account that racks up over 2 million views. The spot opens with a fireball and the line: 'With chronic disease running rampant, President Trump is sending one man.' The Kennedy action figure battles a 'Chronic Disease' Godzilla monster, drinks whole milk, flips the new food pyramid, and dives into a river in 'waterproof jeans.' The ad closes with a 'limited edition Iron Mike Tyson' figure sliding into frame, with Tyson's robotic voice intoning, 'Eat real food or else.' HHS creative director Ryan Nahill, who produced the spot, posts: 'At HHS, we're breaking the internet with one simple message: EAT REAL FOOD.' The video draws both viral mockery and fervent praise from MAHA supporters.
title: RFK Jr. Action Figure Ad Goes Viral — 'Iron Mike Tyson' Edition

description: Bloomberg and CNBC report that key MAHA constituencies, particularly independents and former Democrats, are growing disillusioned with the Trump administration over pesticide policies and the EPA's posture on chemicals. 'Glyphosate Girl' Kelly Ryerson warns: 'These are not loyal Republican voters. They came here because they believed this administration was finally going to stand up to chemical companies. If that doesn't happen, they will absolutely walk.'
title: MAHA Voters Begin Souring — Midterm Warning Signs

description: Kennedy publicly defends Trump's glyphosate executive order, framing it as a matter of national security and agricultural supply chain resilience. In a lengthy social media post he acknowledges pesticides are 'toxic by design' and commits to accelerating the transition to regenerative agriculture, but backs the order as a necessary step given U.S. dependence on foreign-controlled inputs. 'I support President Trump's Executive Order to bring agricultural chemical production back to the United States and end our near-total reliance on adversarial nations,' Kennedy writes. He positions the EO as consistent with the long-term MAHA goal of building a safer food system, promising federal urgency on alternatives including precision weed control, robotics, and biological controls.
title: RFK Jr. Backs Trump on Glyphosate as National Security Issue

description: President Trump invokes the Defense Production Act to compel domestic production of glyphosate-based herbicides, declaring them critical to national security. MAHA advocates are furious. Zen Honeycutt of Moms Across America calls it 'a love letter to glyphosate.' Food activist Vani Hari says it 'reads like it was drafted in a chemical company boardroom.'
title: Trump Signs Glyphosate Executive Order — MAHA Outrage

description: The New York Times reports that the EPA is moving to roll back mercury emission rules for coal-burning power plants, arguing it would reduce 'unwarranted costs' for utilities. Mercury from coal plants is a major source of fish contamination, the same issue RFK Jr. has long prioritized. The administration has simultaneously ordered eight coal units headed for retirement to stay open. The move draws sharp criticism from MAHA-aligned health advocates as a direct contradiction of Kennedy's anti-mercury agenda.
title: EPA Plans to Loosen Mercury Rules for Coal Plants

description: Kennedy and musician Kid Rock release a 90-second HHS-produced video promoting physical activity and whole foods as part of the 'Eat Real Food' campaign. The video features the pair exercising, using an infrared sauna, playing pickleball, and drinking whole milk. The clip accumulated 11.5 million views across HHS social media channels.
title: RFK Jr. & Kid Rock Release HHS Health Promotion Video

description: MAHA Action President Tony Lyons sends a formal strategy memo to RNC, NRSC, and NRCC chairmen (cc'd to Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Speaker Mike Johnson), arguing that MAHA is 'a once in a generation political gift to the GOP,' comparable to MAGA in 2016. New polling from Fabrizio, Lee and Associates identifies two key voter blocs the GOP must activate: the 'MAHA Winnable Middle' (14% of voters, persuadable Democrats and independents who chose a MAHA-framed Republican over a generic Democrat by nearly 2:1) and 'MAHA Rentals' (10%, soft Republicans who back the generic GOP but may stay home if the party ignores MAHA). The memo warns that without embracing MAHA, Republicans risk suppressing friendly turnout, and argues the movement can flip a 5-point generic ballot Democratic lead into a Republican advantage. Top persuasion issues: hospital price transparency, removing petroleum-based food dyes, testing baby formula for heavy metals, and restricting misleading marketing targeting children.
title: MAHA Action Sends GOP Strategy Memo: 'A Once in a Generation Political Gift'

description: The MAHA Center, an advocacy group aligned with Kennedy's HHS agenda, airing a 30-second Super Bowl ad starring Mike Tyson. In the spot, Tyson recounts weighing 345 pounds and consuming 'a quart of ice cream every hour,' and shares that his sister died at 25 from a heart attack linked to obesity. The ad ends with Tyson and his son eating apples, directing viewers to RealFood.gov. It is one of the Super Bowl's most counter-programming moments: a federal health message during America's biggest junk food occasion.
title: Mike Tyson Stars in MAHA Super Bowl Ad

description: Kennedy posts a video to his official HHS social media accounts featuring former heavyweight champion Mike Tyson slapping a donut out of a staffer's hand and declaring, 'What do you think you're doing?! Processed food KILLS.' Tyson, whose sister died at 25 from obesity-related heart failure, tells Fox News he joined willingly: 'I'm one of the most healthiest people on the planet — they should think I will want to be a participant in this.' The clip goes viral, racking up millions of views. The partnership cements Tyson as an unofficial celebrity ambassador for MAHA's 'Eat Real Food' message.
title: Mike Tyson Joins HHS 'Eat Real Food' Campaign

description: The Trump EPA reapproves dicamba, a drift-prone herbicide sprayed on genetically engineered cotton and soybeans, despite federal courts having ruled such approvals unlawful in both 2020 and 2024. Since its first approval in 2016, dicamba drift has damaged millions of acres of farmland, orchards, vegetable farms, and wildlife refuges. Experts call it the worst herbicide drift damage in U.S. agricultural history. The new approval provides even fewer drift protections than past versions. Lawsuits are filed within weeks.
title: EPA Reapproves Dicamba Despite Court Rulings and Drift Damage

description: Three federal agencies committed over $1 billion to modernize U.S. agriculture and reduce chemical dependence: USDA allocated $840M through conservation programs (EQIP, CSP) to fund regenerative agriculture; EPA launched a $30M grand prize challenge for pesticide alternatives to pre-harvest desiccation; and EPA, USDA, and NIH committed to developing a cumulative chemical exposure research framework for the food supply. Rooted in Executive Order 14212 establishing the MAHA Commission.
title: HHS, USDA & EPA Announce $1B+ Farm Modernization Investment

description: Trump EPA reversed Biden-era tightening of the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards, the rule governing emissions from coal-fired power plants and the largest human source of mercury pollution. Coal plant mercury enters the food chain through fish and other food sources. Mercury is a neurotoxin that impairs brain development in young children and contributes to heart attacks in adults. EPA cited "hundreds of millions in savings" for utility operators. Announced at a coal plant on the Ohio River in Louisville, Kentucky.
title: Mercury & Air Toxics Standards (MATS) Rollback

description: EPA reapproved dicamba (described by experts as causing "the worst drift of any herbicide in the history of U.S. agriculture") with fewer protections than previous versions. Eliminated seasonal cutoff dates and temperature-based spray restrictions that had limited its spread. Since 2016, dicamba drift has damaged millions of acres of crops, orchards, vegetable farms, and wildlife refuges. Threatens monarch butterflies and rusty patched bumblebees. Federal courts had struck down two prior EPA approvals (2020, 2024) before this third approval.
title: EPA Reapproves Dicamba With Weakened Restrictions

description: The Trump administration sides with Bayer-Monsanto in a Supreme Court case that could severely limit individuals' ability to sue if they believe they got cancer from glyphosate-based pesticides. MAHA advocates call it a betrayal. 'MAHA moms' warn this could be a breaking point for the movement.
title: Trump Administration Backs Bayer at Supreme Court

description: Kennedy launches a national 'Take Back Your Health' tour, beginning at the Pennsylvania State Capitol in Harrisburg, the first stop of what his office brands an 'Eat Real Food Tour.' He joins over a dozen state legislators to promote the new food pyramid, dietary guidelines, and MAHA's state-by-state legislative agenda. The tour is designed as a hybrid of public health outreach and political messaging, rallying state capitals ahead of the 2026 midterms.
title: 'Take Back Your Health' / 'Eat Real Food' Tour Kicks Off in Pennsylvania

description: Kennedy and USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins released the most significant reset of federal nutrition policy in decades. The 10-page guidelines, down from 164 pages in 2020, explicitly warn against highly processed foods for the first time, introduce an inverted food pyramid prioritizing protein, dairy, and healthy fats, and drop the long-standing low-fat dogma. As the governing standard for the National School Lunch Program, the guidelines directly affect what 30 million children eat daily. Companion site RealFood.gov launched the same day. The guidelines represent a genuine shift in the federal government's official position on diet and chronic disease. However, dietary guidelines are advisory; they carry no regulatory force over what food companies can produce or market, and do not alter the farm subsidies and commodity policies that make ultra-processed food the most affordable option for millions of Americans. Their real-world impact depends heavily on whether they are backed by enforcement mechanisms, school food funding, and changes to agricultural policy that have not yet materialized.
title: Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2025–2030 — "Eat Real Food"

description: After a 'hard fight,' the controversial Bayer-backed pesticide liability provision is removed from the 2026 EPA appropriations bill. Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-ME) credits MAHA-aligned advocates, including Moms Across America founder Zen Honeycutt, with providing critical cross-party pressure on Republican lawmakers. Senate Republicans agree not to revisit it.
title: WIN: Pesticide Liability Rider Stripped from EPA Spending Bill

description: EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced the agency's intent to develop rules eliminating unreasonable risks from five phthalate chemicals (BBP, DBP, DCHP, DEHP, and DIBP) used in plastics and building materials. DEHP alone faces restrictions on 30 conditions of use. Under TSCA, once the EPA identifies unreasonable risk, rulemaking to eliminate that risk is legally required, making this a binding mandate rather than a voluntary commitment.
title: EPA Mandated to Regulate Five Phthalate Chemicals

description: Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, alongside RFK Jr. and CMS Administrator Dr. Oz, launched a $700 million Regenerative Pilot Program ($400M through EQIP and $300M through CSP) to help farmers adopt whole-farm conservation practices addressing soil health, water quality, and natural vitality through a single streamlined application. NRCS established a Chief's Regenerative Agriculture Advisory Council to guide implementation. The program provides farmers an "off-ramp" to transition away from synthetic input dependence.
title: USDA Launches $700M Regenerative Pilot Program

description: Awards were scored in part on state commitments to eight policy actions, including restricting the use of SNAP benefits on non-nutritious foods. A policy analysis says CMS reframed the discretionary funds to align with the administration's Make America Healthy Again agenda; GAO itself does not use the term.
title: CMS Awards $10 Billion to All 50 States, Scored Partly on MAHA-Style Policies

description: The Trump EPA approves isocycloseram, a PFAS 'forever chemical' pesticide, for use on golf courses, lawns, and food crops including oranges, tomatoes, almonds, and oats. It is the second PFAS pesticide approved in two weeks, with three more planned. The EPA waives a standard child-safety buffer despite the pesticide's links to reduced sperm count, reduced testicle size, and liver toxicity. The pesticide office is controlled by two former lobbyists for the American Chemistry Council. Critics note the approvals directly contradict MAHA's stated mission to protect children from toxic chemical exposures.
title: EPA Approves Second 'Forever Chemical' Pesticide in Two Weeks

description: A high-profile invitation-only MAHA summit is held at the Waldorf Astoria in Washington. VP JD Vance attends and calls MAHA 'a critical part of our success in Washington.' The event signals the movement's continued relevance to GOP electoral strategy ahead of 2026 midterms.
title: MAHA Summit at Waldorf Astoria — VP Vance Attends

description: Trump EPA approved isocycloseram for use on food crops (oranges, tomatoes, almonds, peas, oats), golf courses, and lawns, despite being a PFAS "forever chemical" that breaks down into 40 additional PFAS compounds. Linked to reduced sperm count, smaller testicle size, and liver toxicity. The approval omitted a child-safety buffer despite children's heightened sensitivity. Bees near treated fields may be exposed to 1,500 times the lethal dose. The second PFAS pesticide approved by this EPA within two weeks.
title: EPA Approves Isocycloseram — A PFAS Pesticide

description: HHS releases the commission's strategy report with more than 120 initiatives to reverse the childhood chronic disease crisis, covering diet, environmental chemicals, physical activity, and overmedicalization. Critics note the report omits calls to reduce pesticide exposure, reportedly after EPA officials intervened.
title: MAHA Commission Releases 'Make Our Children Healthy Again' Strategy

description: EPA renewed glyphosate's pesticide registration for 15 years despite ~181,000 pending cancer lawsuits (non-Hodgkin's lymphoma), a $2.1 billion Georgia jury verdict, and the Trump DOJ filing a brief urging the Supreme Court to side with Bayer and strip cancer victims of their right to sue under state law. MAHA supporters had previously blocked a glyphosate liability shield from an appropriations rider; the administration then did the opposite. Cross-partisan response: Rep. Thomas Massie's No Immunity for Glyphosate Act, co-sponsored by Pingree, Boebert, Mace, and Khanna, would restore victims' right to sue, but has not advanced to a floor vote.
title: EPA Glyphosate Registration Review

description: A House appropriations bill for the EPA includes language that would bar states and courts from penalizing pesticide makers for failing to include health warnings beyond those recognized by the EPA, effectively shielding Roundup/glyphosate maker Bayer from failure-to-warn lawsuits. MAHA groups call it a 'liability shield.'
title: House Appropriations Pesticide Rider Ignites MAHA Backlash

description: The 2025 reconciliation law created a program of up to $50 billion over five years for rural health while cutting roughly $911 billion from Medicaid over ten years, per KFF figures cited by The New Republic. The Bipartisan Policy Center notes the program is not designed to directly replace the funding cut in H.R. 1. The $911 billion figure is secondary and should be verified against KFF directly.
title: Reconciliation Law Cuts Medicaid and Creates the Rural Health Transformation Program

description: Signed by Gov. Jeff Landry (R), SB 14 bans 15 food additives, including synthetic dyes and preservatives, from school meals starting the 2028–29 school year. The law also requires physicians and nurse practitioners to complete continuing education in nutrition and metabolic health, and mandates that food manufacturers attach a QR code to products containing any of 44 listed ingredients, giving consumers direct access to ingredient safety information at the point of purchase.
title: SB 14 / Act 463 — School Food Additive Ban & Labeling

description: EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin moves to continue allowing dicamba, expand PFAS-containing pesticides, and resist pesticide restrictions, directly contradicting MAHA priorities. MAHA activists circulate a petition demanding Trump fire Zeldin. The EPA's posture is widely described as 'misaligned' with HHS and USDA.
title: MAHA-MAGA Rift Opens Over EPA Pesticide Policy

description: Kennedy campaign veterans Mark Gorton and Tony Lyons formally launch the MAHA Institute in Washington, D.C., rebranding the 501(c)(4) wing of their American Values Super PAC into a permanent policy and advocacy organization. Described as a rival to established think tanks, the Institute is designed to translate grassroots MAHA energy into legislative and regulatory action. Its stated mission: connect the movement's 110,000+ supporters with the roughly 75 true MAHA allies inside a 60,000-person HHS bureaucracy. Calley Means, White House health adviser, calls it a 'generational opportunity.' Zen Honeycutt of Moms Across America and Mary Holland of Children's Health Defense are among the founding coalition.
title: MAHA Institute Launches in Washington

description: Signed by Gov. Greg Abbott (R), SB 314 bans 17 food additives from school lunches starting the 2026–27 school year and establishes a statewide Nutrition Advisory Committee. A companion labeling law, the first of its kind in the U.S., requires warning labels on any food product sold in Texas that contains ingredients banned or restricted in Australia, Canada, the EU, or the UK. Companies must either add the warning, reformulate, or stop selling affected products in Texas. The labeling requirement is expected to create national pressure on manufacturers to reformulate.
title: SB 314 — School Food Ban & First-in-Nation Additive Warning Labels

description: Shields pesticide manufacturers from failure-to-warn lawsuits as long as federal label requirements are met, effectively protecting Bayer's Roundup from state court liability. Georgia becomes the second state to pass such a law, following North Dakota. A Georgia jury had awarded a cancer plaintiff $2.1 billion in March 2025, just before the law's passage. Bayer faces ~181,000 glyphosate-cancer claims nationally.
title: Pesticide Liability Protection Act (Glyphosate Shield)

description: The Democratic National Committee and independent analysts flag multiple citations in a draft MAHA commission report as nonexistent, citing evidence of AI-generated sourcing errors. The White House calls them 'formatting issues.' The episode damages the report's credibility and fuels broader criticism of the commission's rigor.
title: MAHA Commission Report Criticized for Fake Citations

description: Kennedy and FDA Commissioner Marty Makary announce a plan to eliminate all petroleum-based synthetic dyes from the U.S. food supply by end of 2026. The FDA will revoke authorization for dyes not in production and establish timelines for remaining dyes. Major companies including Nestlé, Hershey, and PepsiCo pledge to comply.
title: FDA Announces Phase-Out of All Synthetic Food Dyes

description: Termination notices go out to thousands of HHS staffers. At the FDA, 3,500 jobs are eliminated, including top regulatory officials. Entire offices (communications, FOIA, infertility research) are shuttered. Former FDA leaders across both parties warn that institutional capacity has been irreparably damaged.
title: Mass HHS Layoffs Execute — FDA, CDC, NIH Hit Hard

description: Trump EPA initiated formal review to weaken or suspend Biden's PFAS drinking water standards, potentially stripping protections for the 100+ million Americans in communities with PFAS-contaminated water systems.
title: PFAS Drinking Water Rule Rollback

description: HHS confirms the clawback of $11.4 billion in COVID-era funds from state and local health departments. Public health clinics are canceled across the country amid a measles outbreak in Texas that kills two children. Critics argue the cuts directly contradict MAHA's child health goals.
title: HHS Claws Back $11.4 Billion in CDC Grants

description: Eliminated Biden-era Waters of the United States rule, removing federal protections for an estimated 51% of the nation's wetlands and many seasonal streams, the waters that filter drinking supplies for millions of Americans.
title: WOTUS Rule Elimination

description: West Virginia becomes the first state to ban seven synthetic food dyes under a new law signed by the governor. The bill is sponsored by a Republican legislator motivated by his foster children's health. Around the same time, roughly 75 dye-related bills are introduced across 37 states.
title: HB 2354 — School Food Dye Restrictions

description: The Senate confirms Kennedy along party lines, 52–48. The same day, President Trump signs an executive order establishing the Make America Healthy Again Commission, chaired by Kennedy. The commission is directed to examine childhood chronic disease, ultra-processed foods, environmental chemicals, and overmedicalization.
title: RFK Jr. Confirmed as HHS Secretary (52–48)

description: Trump EPA withdrew proposed rules that would have required factory farms to reduce discharge of ammonia, pathogens, and pharmaceuticals into waterways, eliminating water quality protections for communities near industrial livestock operations.
title: EPA CAFO Effluent Guideline Withdrawal

description: DOGE teams begin reviewing HHS contracts and grants. Approximately 10,000 HHS employees depart through voluntary separation. A second wave of 10,000 layoff notices follows in late March–April, cutting roughly 20–31% of the federal public health workforce across FDA, CDC, and NIH. Critics warn this undercuts MAHA's own stated goals.
title: DOGE Targets HHS — Mass Layoffs Begin

description: Kennedy appears before the Senate Finance Committee and the HELP Committee. His views on pharmaceutical regulation and federal health agency reform draw bipartisan scrutiny. Sen. Mitch McConnell is among those voicing concerns. 'MAHA moms' flood Senate phone lines in support.
title: RFK Jr. Confirmation Hearings

description: FDA revoked authorization for Red Dye No. 3 (erythrosine) in food and ingested drugs, a synthetic dye linked to thyroid tumors in animal studies, after the Delaney Clause required removal once carcinogenicity was demonstrated. Manufacturers given 2 years to reformulate.
title: FDA Bans Red Dye No. 3

description: Sen. Roger Marshall (R-KS) launches the Make America Healthy Again Caucus in the Senate to support the joint mission of Trump and Kennedy. It represents the formal legislative arm of the movement on Capitol Hill.
title: Senate MAHA Caucus Launched

description: Under current FDA rules, food companies can self-certify new food additives as "Generally Recognized as Safe" (GRAS) without notifying or seeking approval from the agency. Thousands of chemicals have entered the U.S. food supply through this pathway without independent government safety review. The Biden FDA acknowledged the problem but took no action to reform the process. At a December 2024 Senate hearing, FDA Commissioner Robert Califf defended inaction, citing legal risk and limited staff. Scientists and legal experts at Harvard characterized the GRAS system as "a laissez-faire approach to monitoring ingredient safety" that poses a direct threat to public health.
title: FDA Takes No Action on GRAS Loophole Throughout Biden Term

description: President-elect Trump nominates Kennedy as Secretary of Health and Human Services, giving MAHA its highest-ever institutional foothold. The nomination draws bipartisan scrutiny in the Senate over Kennedy's views on food safety, pharmaceutical regulation, and the role of federal health agencies.
title: Trump Nominates RFK Jr. to Lead HHS

description: Donald Trump wins the presidency. MAHA-aligned voters are credited as a meaningful coalition contribution, particularly independents and former Democrats who crossed over based on health and food safety concerns.
title: Trump Elected 47th President

description: Trump welcomes Kennedy to the stage at a Turning Point Action rally in Duluth, Georgia, cementing the MAHA-MAGA alliance before a national audience and signaling Kennedy's future role in a potential Trump administration.
title: Trump Brings RFK Jr. Onstage at Campaign Rally

description: The Senate roundtable "American Health and Nutrition: A Second Opinion" takes place in the Kennedy Caucus Room at the Russell Senate Office Building. The full session is livestreamed and later released publicly. It signals growing congressional interest in MAHA ideas ahead of the election.
title: Johnson Roundtable Held — Full Video Released

description: Sen. Ron Johnson (R-WI) issues a media advisory announcing a nonpartisan roundtable titled "American Health and Nutrition: A Second Opinion," to be held September 23 in the Russell Senate Office Building. The event features Dr. Casey Means, Calley Means, Jordan Peterson, Vani Hari (Food Babe), Jillian Michaels, and other MAHA-aligned voices.
title: Sen. Ron Johnson Announces 'A Second Opinion' Roundtable

description: FDA issued proposed rule for mandatory front-of-package "nutrition info" labeling, including a "high in" warning label for sodium, saturated fat, and added sugars, representing the most significant food labeling reform in decades.
title: FDA Front-of-Package Labeling Proposal

description: Banned six synthetic food dyes (Red 40, Yellow 5, Yellow 6, Blue 1, Blue 2, and Green 3) from all meals, drinks, and snacks served at California public schools statewide. First state-level school food dye ban in the U.S. Manufacturers required to reformulate products with natural alternatives by December 2027.
title: AB 2316 — California School Food Safety Act

description: Kennedy suspends his independent presidential bid at a press conference in Phoenix and endorses Donald Trump, uniting the MAHA coalition with MAGA and marrying health freedom politics with conservative electoral power. Kennedy delivers a bloc of voters focused on food safety, chronic disease, and reform of federal health agencies.
title: RFK Jr. Suspends Campaign & Endorses Trump

description: The phrase "Make America Healthy Again" officially enters the political lexicon, championed by Kennedy's campaign. The movement draws from the "health freedom" movement that grew during the COVID-19 pandemic, uniting clean food advocates and critics of Big Pharma, Big Agriculture, and corporate capture of federal health agencies.
title: The MAHA Slogan Is Born

description: Banned PFAS in food packaging, food service ware, and cookware sold in Washington, among the strongest state PFAS restrictions in the country, with phased implementation for different product categories.
title: PFAS Food Packaging Restriction Act

description: Included provisions preempting local government authority to restrict pesticide use beyond state minimums, eliminating local organic zones, pesticide-free parks, and school buffer restrictions. Backed heavily by the agricultural chemical industry.
title: SB 1084 — Pesticide Preemption Provision

description: Codified Gov. Reynolds' executive order prohibiting the Iowa DNR from strengthening CAFO regulations, permanently blocking tighter rules on factory farm siting, particularly in environmentally sensitive karst terrain where contamination of groundwater is most severe. Passed 91-3 in the House.
title: SF 2370 — CAFO Rulemaking Preemption

description: First-ever enforceable federal limits on six PFAS compounds in drinking water, covering an estimated 100+ million Americans. Set maximum contaminant levels for PFOA, PFOS, and four other "forever chemicals" linked to cancer and immune disruption.
title: EPA PFAS Drinking Water Standards

description: Strengthened school meal requirements: reduced sodium limits over 5-year phase-in, required whole grain minimums, and capped added sugars in school breakfasts for the first time, affecting 30 million children daily.
title: USDA School Meal Nutrition Standards Update

description: A 2024 analysis identified 66 active pesticide ingredients registered with the EPA between 1972 and 2021 that meet the OECD definition of PFAS, "forever chemicals" that do not break down in the environment. California agricultural fields alone are sprayed with an average of 2.5 million pounds of PFAS pesticides per year. Many of these ingredients break down into trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), which is increasingly detected in groundwater and linked to liver toxicity. Throughout the Biden term, the EPA continued approving these compounds without assessing cumulative TFA contamination risks or treating PFAS pesticides as a class.
title: Biden EPA Continued Registering PFAS-Containing Pesticides

description: Banned neonicotinoid-treated corn, soybean, and wheat seeds, plus neonicotinoid use on outdoor ornamental plants and turf. Targets imidacloprid, thiamethoxam, and acetamiprid, the chemicals the EPA identified as driving "more than 200 species toward extinction." Called "nation-leading" by Hochul; Vermont and other states moving to follow.
title: S.1856-A — Birds and Bees Protection Act

description: Republican-negotiated Farm Bill provisions tightened SNAP work requirements and eligibility, reducing food access for an estimated 750,000 households, disproportionately in rural food deserts and among formerly incarcerated individuals.
title: Farm Bill SNAP Eligibility Restrictions

description: Kennedy ends his Democratic primary challenge and re-enters the race as an independent at a rally in Philadelphia. His platform increasingly emphasizes food systems, toxic chemicals, and the chronic disease epidemic, positioning MAHA-style ideas as a cross-partisan cause.
title: RFK Jr. Relaunches as Independent Candidate

description: Banned four harmful food additives (Red Dye No. 3, Titanium Dioxide, Potassium Bromate, and Brominated Vegetable Oil) from food sold in California. The strongest state food additive law in U.S. history, affecting product formulations nationwide.
title: AB 418 — California Food Safety Act

description: Strengthened housing habitability enforcement, making landlords liable for unsafe conditions including mold, faulty smoke detectors, and substandard ventilation. Added mandatory pre-move walk-through inspections to document health hazards before occupancy. Mold exposure is associated with respiratory illness, asthma, and immune dysfunction, disproportionately affecting low-income renters.
title: SB 998 — Tenant Protections & Habitability Act

description: Robert F. Kennedy Jr. formally declares his candidacy for the Democratic presidential nomination at the Park Plaza Hotel in Boston. His campaign centers on ending the 'corrupt merger of state and corporate power,' chronic disease, and food safety: the ideological seeds of MAHA.
title: RFK Jr. Launches Presidential Campaign

description: The Biden administration approved ConocoPhillips' Willow Project, a 30-year, $8 billion oil drilling operation in Alaska's National Petroleum Reserve, despite more than 3 million petition signatures in opposition and Biden's own 2020 pledge to end new drilling on federal lands. The scaled-down approval authorizes three drill pads and up to 150 oil wells, projected to produce 180,000 barrels per day at peak and generate approximately 260 million metric tons of carbon emissions over the project's lifetime. The decision drew immediate legal challenges from environmental groups and illustrated the gap between the administration's climate commitments and its energy policy decisions.
title: Biden Administration Approves Willow Project Oil Drilling in Alaska's Arctic

description: In January 2023, the Biden EPA announced it would postpone setting Effluent Limitation Guidelines, rules that cap how much PFAS industry can discharge into rivers, lakes, and waterways. The delay left a primary source of PFAS contamination unregulated, with no binding restrictions on industrial discharge. Environmental groups had documented PFAS entering drinking water sources downstream of manufacturing facilities. The guidelines were never finalized during the Biden term, leaving the gap in place when the administration ended.
title: Biden EPA Delays PFAS Industrial Discharge Limits

description: Included $20 billion for voluntary conservation programs, including restrictions on certain pesticide-adjacent practices and incentives for reducing synthetic input use on farmland, the largest federal conservation investment in history.
title: Inflation Reduction Act — Conservation Provisions

description: Biden EPA finalized a ban on chlorpyrifos, a neurotoxic organophosphate pesticide linked to childhood neurological damage, for all agricultural food uses, after decades of industry lobbying blocked action under prior administrations.
title: EPA Chlorpyrifos Agricultural Ban

description: First state to ban spreading municipal sludge (a major source of PFAS) on farmland and to phase out PFAS in pesticides and adjuvants by 2030. Created a $60 million farmer assistance fund for health monitoring, income replacement, and buyouts for irreparably contaminated farms. No other state had done either before Maine.
title: LD 2013 & LD 1911 — PFAS Agricultural Laws
